item.title: Progressive outer midbrain lesion associated with repetitive mild traumatic brain injury: a study of 52 professional wrestlers.
item.description:
J Neurosurg | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Spine, TBI] [strong match]
Yamamoto A, Sasaki M, Hijikata Y et al.

OBJECTIVE: Finite element modeling studies suggest that the midbrain is susceptible to mechanical strain during mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), but clinical neuroimaging characterization of midbrain alterations associated with mTBI remains limited. In 2018, the authors identified lesions on T2-weighted MRI consistently localized in the lateral midbrain tegmentum of some veteran professional Japanese wrestlers. These lesions were termed outer midbrain lesions (OMLs). This study aimed to elucidate the relationship between mTBI and OMLs.

METHODS: The study included 52 male Japanese professional wrestlers who underwent brain MRI examinations in 2022. An OML was defined as a lesion with a diameter ≥ 2 mm. Longitudinal changes in OMLs were examined in wrestlers who had undergone MRI before 2022. As a control group, brain MRI data from 91 patients with spinal cord injury or central poststroke pain from the authors' prior study were reviewed for the presence of OMLs. Wrestling career length was investigated as a surrogate for the period of repetitive head impact. Histories of concussion and symptomatic mTBI were reviewed from the records maintained by exclusive trainers.

RESULTS: OMLs were identified in 12 wrestlers (23.1%). Traumatic lesions were not observed in other parts of the brain. OMLs were identified only in wrestlers older than 40 years, whereas they were absent in the control group, even among older individuals. OMLs exhibited progressive growth over time on longitudinal MRI. The presence of OMLs was not associated with a documented history of symptomatic mTBI, but with career length. Each additional year of participation in professional wrestling was associated with a 14% increase in the prevalence of OMLs (prevalence ratio 1.14, 95% CI 1.08-1.19).

CONCLUSIONS: OMLs are neural structural alterations strongly suggested to be associated with repeated asymptomatic mTBI. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate the susceptibility of the midbrain to mTBI based on real-world clinical findings.

item.title: Calculating trauma undertriage rates: Are we using the wrong formula-and the wrong definition?
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Prehospital, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Scott T, Orlando A, Shen Y et al.

BACKGROUND: Undertriage (UT) is central to trauma center quality improvement, yet UT definitions vary, and no data-driven consensus target exists for interfacility benchmarking. We compared facility-level UT rates across four methods and assessed the impact on facility benchmarking.

METHODS: This retrospective study included patients aged 18 to 89 from Level I & II trauma centers in the ACS TQP Files (2021-2023). Facility-level UT was calculated using the Cribari Matrix Method (CMM), modified Cribari Matrix Method (mCMM), Standardized Triage Assessment Tool (STAT), and High-Intensity Time-Sensitive (HITS) intervention-based definition representing trauma team actions. Paired facility-level UT rates were compared across methods. To estimate benchmarking impact, we calculated within-facility rank change (higher rank = higher UT) relative to CMM.

RESULTS: 2,643,881 patients and 515 facilities were included. Median facility-level UT significantly differed by method: CMM 11% [interquartile range: 9-14], mCMM 60% [50-67], STAT 6% [5-8], and HITS 30% [22-40] (all P<0.001). At individual hospitals, the median range of maximum UT values between methods was 53% [44-60]. The median absolute facility rank change between the CMM method and other tools was 129 [54.5-236.5] for mCMM, 48 [17-90] for STAT, and 142 [62.5-252.5] for HITS.

CONCLUSIONS: These UT data highlight a concerning level of variation and uncertainty in the calculation and interpretation of a key trauma center performance metric. Until a UT definition is standardized and data-driven UT target goals established, cross-center benchmarking using UT should be interpreted cautiously and may be better suited for within-center trending.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic/care management.

item.title: Bougie guided versus Endotracheal tube with Stylet guided intubation in critically injured patients with Difficult airway characteristics (BEST trial): randomised clinical trial.
item.description:
Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med | Core Trauma [General Trauma] [weak match]
Goyal A, Kacchap S, Singla K et al.

BACKGROUND: Emergency airway management in critically injured trauma patients is frequently complicated by distorted anatomy, airway contamination, cervical spine immobilisation, and prior airway manipulation. Although bougie and stylet are commonly used adjuncts for tracheal intubation, evidence comparing their effectiveness in difficult trauma airways remains limited. We aimed to compare first-pass intubation success between bougie-guided and stylet-guided tracheal intubation in critically injured trauma patients with predefined difficult airway characteristics.

METHODS: In this prospective randomised clinical trial, 188 adult critically injured trauma patients requiring emergency tracheal intubation and having at least one predefined difficult airway characteristic were randomised to bougie-guided intubation (Group B, n = 94) or stylet-guided intubation (Group S, n = 94). All first-attempt intubations were performed by trauma anaesthesia senior residents using video laryngoscopy and a standardised drug-assisted delayed sequence intubation protocol. The primary outcome was first-pass intubation success. Secondary outcomes included time to intubation, rescue airway interventions, need for alternate adjunct or front-of-neck access, and peri-intubation complications.

RESULTS: First-pass intubation success was achieved in 67 of 94 patients (71.3%) in Group B and 63 of 94 patients (67.0%) in Group S, corresponding to an absolute difference of 4.3% points (95% CI, - 8.9 to 17.2; p = 0.53). Time to successful first-attempt intubation was similar between groups (39.55 ± 11.72 s in Group B versus 37.97 ± 13.54 s in Group S; mean difference 1.58 s, 95% CI - 2.80 to 5.97; p = 0.48). Emergency front-of-neck access was required in one patient in Group B. Oesophageal intubation occurred in five patients (5.3%) in Group S and in none in Group B; this difference did not reach statistical significance using Fisher's exact test (p = 0.059). On multivariable logistic regression, polytrauma with facial fractures was associated with increased odds of first-pass intubation failure (adjusted OR 2.54, 95% CI 1.10-5.83; p = 0.028).

CONCLUSION: In selected trauma patients with predefined difficult-airway characteristics undergoing protocolised delayed sequence intubation with video laryngoscopy, no statistically significant difference in first-pass success was observed between bougie-guided and stylet-guided intubation. Oesophageal intubation occurred only in the stylet group, an exploratory finding that requires confirmation in larger studies.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: The trial was approved by the Institute Ethics Committee (IEC-INT-2022/MD-543) and registered with the Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI/2022/11/047043).

item.title: Development and validation of methods to predict ground- and helicopter-based emergency medical service travel times.
item.description:
Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med | Core Trauma [weak match]
Spangler D, Sheffield J, Alm J et al.

BACKGROUND: Helicopter-based Emergency Medical Services (EMS) are a costly and finite resource and should only be deployed when they provide substantial benefits to patients. One such benefit is a more rapid response to incidents and transport to hospital compared to Ground-based EMS. This study evaluates methods for estimating travel times for the purpose of optimizing the selection of helicopter vs. ground EMS.

METHODS: Ground EMS travel times were estimated using an open-source routing tool, the estimates of which were adjusted using linear regression and gradient boosting models based on historical travel times. Helicopter travel times were similarly estimated based on great circle distances adjusted by historical data. Models were evaluated using several measures of predictive accuracy to enable comparison with other studies.

RESULTS: In validation data collected after finalization of the methods, the best performing prediction models for Ground EMS travel times explained a substantial portion of variation in drive times to location and to hospital (R2 0.79 and 0.70 respectively), and less for helicopter flight times (R2 0.46 and 0.38 respectively). Mean average percentage error was 18-20% for all investigated estimation techniques and time intervals.

CONCLUSION: Integrating tools based on the open-source code provided with this study has the potential to improve the ability of dispatchers to estimate relative travel times and assess the potential time benefit of directing the most appropriate resources to a given patient.

item.title: The association of ABO Rh blood groups with 30-day mortality following traumatic injury - A retrospective observational study in the East of England.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Li J, Bell R, Basheer B et al.

BACKGROUND: ABO and RhD antigens are expressed on the surface of red blood cells; ABO antigens are also expressed on the surface of endothelial and some epithelial cells. Associations between ABO blood groups and disease have been reported in numerous areas of medicine. Recently there have been conflicting reports of an association between blood group O and mortality following trauma, none of which examine a combination of ABO and RhD groups. The aim of our study was to identify associations between all ABO RhD groups and trauma mortality.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis of trauma patients ≥ 16-years-old admitted to the East of England Major Trauma Centre, and who were included in the Trauma, Audit, & Research Network (TARN) database, 2016-2019. The primary outcome was a comparison of 30-day all-cause mortality between all eight ABO RhD groups. Secondary outcomes included injury pattern analysis on outcome.

RESULTS: 4188 patients were included; median age 59.3 [IQR 39.0-77.9] years old, and 2634 (62.9%) were male. The median injury severity score was 19.0 [10.0-25.0]. 30-day mortality was 9.3%, and there were significant differences in mortality across groups (p = 0.0094). O negative was associated with greater 30-day mortality compared to all other seven ABO RhD groups combined: 15.1% vs 8.8%; relative risk (RR) 1.7 (95%CI 1.3-2.2), p = 0.0002.

CONCLUSIONS: In this UK study we have demonstrated that blood group O negative is associated with a greater risk of 30-day all-cause mortality in undifferentiated trauma patients. Future trauma studies should consider including ABO RhD blood group as a baseline characteristic to ensure this does not confound results.

item.title: Thoracic epidural versus paravertebral blockade for reducing chronic post-thoracotomy pain (TOPIC-2): open label, parallel group, superiority, multicentre, randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BMJ | Tier 2 Filtered [Thoracic] [strong match]
Shelley B, Middleton L, Boyles R et al.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effectiveness of paravertebral blockade versus thoracic epidural during the perioperative period in reducing chronic post-thoracotomy pain.

DESIGN: Open label, parallel group, superiority, multicentre, randomised controlled trial.

SETTING: 15 thoracic centres in the UK.

PARTICIPANTS: Adult patients undergoing thoracotomy randomised (1:1) to either paravertebral blockade or thoracic epidural using a web based service between January 2019 and September 2023.

INTERVENTIONS: Participants in the paravertebral group received three single-shot paravertebral injections of local anaesthetic before incision

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE: The primary outcome was incidence of chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six months after randomisation, defined as a 100 mm visual analogue score greater than or equal to 40 mm (indicating moderate pain) when considering worst chest pain over the past week. Secondary outcomes included acute pain (visual analogue score of 100 mm) and complications.

RESULTS: 770 patients were enrolled, of which 428 (56%) were male (mean (standard deviation, SD) age 66.6 (11.0) years). After 33 exclusions of patients after randomisation who did not proceed to thoracotomy, 737 remained in the modified intention-to-treat population (364 in the paravertebral group, 373 in the epidural group). Six months after randomisation, 59 (22%) of 272 participants in the paravertebral group and 47 (16%) of 292 participants in the epidural group developed chronic post-thoracotomy pain (adjusted risk ratio 1.32 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.93 to 1.86), adjusted risk difference 0.05 (95% CI -0.01 to 0.11), P=0.12). During the acute phase, worst and average pain was greater on day 1 with paravertebral blockade (adjusted mean difference 7.7 mm (95% CI 2.8 to 12.5 mm) and 7.0 mm (95% CI 2.7 to 11.2 mm), respectively), but no different on days 2-3. Hypotension was less common in the paravertebral group than the epidural group (12%

CONCLUSIONS: Paravertebral blockade did not reduce chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six month follow-up compared to thoracic epidural. Thoracic epidural provided marginally better acute pain relief one day after the operation, but showed no difference thereafter. Postoperative complications were comparable between groups. The findings support the ongoing use of both techniques.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03677856.

item.title: Is surgeon technique a modifiable risk factor for heterotopic ossification after posterior acetabular fracture fixation? A multi-surgeon study.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, TBI] [weak match]
Kumar DS, Luther L, Schaffer NE et al.

INTRODUCTION: Heterotopic ossification (HO) is a well-recognized complication following operative fixation of acetabular fractures through a posterior approach. Established risk factors largely reflect nonmodifiable patient and injury characteristics. Whether surgeon-controlled aspects of operative technique influence HO remains poorly defined. The purpose of this study was to determine if the individual surgeon and specific technique variables are associated with HO after accounting for established patient and injury factors.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 1292 patients who underwent acetabular fracture fixation through a Kocher-Langenbeck approach at two Level 1 trauma centers between 2010 and 2025 by 14 fellowship-trained orthopaedic traumatologists. Patients receiving any form of HO prophylaxis were excluded. Four surgeon-controlled variables were examined: aggressiveness of gluteus minimus debridement, trochanteric osteotomy, thrombin gel use, and closed suction drainage. HO was graded on final radiographs by two independent reviewers using the Brooker classification, with third-reader adjudication for disagreements, and categorized as little-to-no (grade 0-I), moderate (grade II), or severe (grade III-IV). Mixed-effects logistic regression models with surgeon as a random effect were used to assess the associations between patient, injury, and surgeon-controlled technique variables, as well as the individual surgeon, with severe and moderate HO formation.

RESULTS: Little-to-no HO occurred in 1132 patients (87.6%), moderate HO in 96 (7.4%), and severe HO in 64 (5.0%). Aggressive gluteus minimus debridement was not associated with HO severity. For severe HO, the surgeon did not contribute meaningfully to model performance, and no surgeon-controlled technique variables were significant; severe head injury, mechanical ventilation beyond 72 h, African-American race, and dual surgical approaches were associated with severe HO. For moderate HO, the surgeon contributed moderately, and both trochanteric osteotomy (odds ratio [OR] 3.7, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.1-12) and closed suction drainage (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.0-3.1) were associated with increased odds of moderate HO.

CONCLUSION: Severe HO following posterior acetabular fracture fixation is predominantly driven by patient and injury characteristics rather than surgeon technique. Aggressive gluteus minimus debridement does not appear to reduce HO risk, and prevention efforts should prioritize patient-level risk stratification.

item.title: Association between mechanical ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure and outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
item.description:
Am J Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [Prehospital] [weak match]
Duchatelet C, Tackaert T, Vanwulpen M et al.

AIM: The effect of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) during intermittent positive pressure ventilation in patients undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on outcome is unknown. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between the use of PEEP during cardiopulmonary resuscitation and clinical outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients.

METHODS: We conducted a single-centre observational cohort study using a retrospective analysis of data collected prospectively within a dedicated research registry of adult OHCA patients managed by a physician-staffed prehospital emergency medical team. All included patients were intubated and ventilated either with mechanical ventilation using PEEP or with manual ventilation without PEEP. Intratracheal pressure was continuously recorded via a catheter connected to a portable device, allowing objective verification of PEEP application and ventilation rate. The association between mechanical ventilation with PEEP use and clinical outcomes was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for relevant confounders.

RESULTS: 362 patients were included, with a median age of 65 years (54-79), of whom 250 (69.1%) were male. Median ventilation rate was 15 breaths/min (10-19). Of all patients, 149 (41.2%) achieved Return Of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC) and 31 (8.6%) survived to hospital discharge. The adjusted odds ratio (OR) of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for achieving ROSC was 1.58 (95% CI 1.01-2.50, p = 0.048). The unadjusted OR of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for survival to hospital discharge was 2.22 (95% CI 1.03-4.78; p = 0.037).

CONCLUSION: The use of mechanical ventilation with PEEP during CPR in OHCA patients was associated with higher likelihood of ROSC.

item.title: PIEZO1 activation alters membrane remodeling and aggregability of stored red blood cells.
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma] [weak match]
Wetmore GC, Wattley LJ, Becker ER et al.

BACKGROUND: Transfused red blood cells (RBCs) actively contribute to post-injury hemostasis due to surface phosphatidylserine (PS) exposure. We hypothesized that storage sensitizes erythrocytes to the PIEZO1-induced, calcium‑dependent, PS externalization through calcium and protein kinase C (PKC) dependent activation of the phospholipid scramblase TMEM16F.

METHODS: Five units of type O whole blood were obtained for analysis at days 21 and 42 of storage. RBC PS was quantified by annexin V staining on flow cytometry at increasing extracellular CaCl₂ concentrations (0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 5.0 mmol/L), with and without the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 (0.2 μM), PKC agonist Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA; 6 μM) and antagonist chelerythrine chloride (CC; 10 μM), and the TMEM16 family inhibitor niclosamide (2 μM). RBC aggregometry was assessed by multiplate. Data were analyzed by analysis of variance and mixed-effects modeling.

RESULTS: PS exposure increased in a Ca²⁺‑dependent manner in both day 21 and 42 RBCs (p<0.001). PIEZO1 stimulation enhanced this response to a greater extent in day 42 RBCs, with greater change in PS at 1 mmol/L (2.21% vs. -0.44%, p=0.021), 2 mmol/L (7.36% vs. 0.53%, p<0.001), and 5 mmol/L (12.09% vs. 6.40%, p<0.001) CaCl2. Compared with calcium alone, Yoda1 and PMA (+61.3%, p<0.001 for both) produced similar increases in PS externalization, whereas PKC inhibition (-45.6%, p=0.009) and TMEM16F inhibition (-4.6%, p=0.99) negated the PIEZO1 response. Yoda1 agonism preserved RBC aggregability after 42 days of storage (51.2±39.0 vs. 2.0±3.5 area under the curve, p<0.001).

CONCLUSION: Storage sensitizes RBCs to PIEZO1-mediated, calcium-dependent, PS externalization through PKC- and TMEM16F-dependent signaling. Given its endogenous mechanosensitive properties, pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation highlights a potential mechanism by which mechanical stress encountered during trauma and transfusion through the injured microcirculation may promote erythrocyte phospholipid membrane remodeling and aggregability, contributing to the procoagulant activity of transfused RBCs.

item.title: Persistent gaps in health-related quality of life measures for older adult trauma patients: A systematic review.
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Orthopaedic, Spine] [strong match]
Haines KL, Park E, Shin GJ et al.

BACKGROUND: Older adults experience persistent functional and psychosocial consequences after trauma, but it remains unclear whether commonly used health-related quality of life (HRQoL) instruments adequately measure recovery in this population. This systematic review appraised psychometric evidence and risk of bias for HRQoL instruments used in United States trauma cohorts that included adults aged 65 years or older.

METHODS: MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL were searched from inception through January 28, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias was evaluated using an adapted Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies-of Interventions (ROBINS-I) assessment. Studies evaluating an HRQoL instrument as the target measure underwent Consensus-based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) Risk of Bias assessment for each reported measurement property. Results were rated as sufficient, insufficient, or indeterminate and synthesized by instrument.

RESULTS: Of 17,195 records, 19 studies were included. Studies most often examined isolated orthopedic trauma (n=7, 36.8%), spinal cord injury (n=6, 31.6%), other injury populations (n=3, 15.8%), polytrauma or systemic injury (n=2, 10.5%), and burns (n=1, 5.3%). Frequently evaluated domains included physical functioning (n=16), emotional or mental health (n=13), overall life satisfaction (n=13), social functioning (n=11), and physical symptoms (n=10). Although all studies used at least one previously developed patient-reported measure, none explicitly adapted or comprehensively validated an eligible HRQoL instrument for older adult trauma patients. Ten studies evaluated a target HRQoL instrument, contributing 33 COSMIN measurement property assessments: 19 sufficient, 10 indeterminate, and 4 insufficient. Overall risk of bias was low in six studies, moderate in eight, serious in three, and unclear in two.

CONCLUSIONS: Existing studies show that HRQoL instruments have been used in trauma cohorts including older adults, but they do not establish validity for older adult trauma patients specifically. Future studies should evaluate promising instruments in cohorts designed around older adults' recovery priorities and clinical characteristics after trauma.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Systematic Review; Level III.

item.title: Blood-Based Biomarkers and Traumatic Intracranial Hypertension: A Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury Study.
item.description:
Neurosurgery | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, TBI] [strong match]
Bonow RH, Temkin N, Barber J et al.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The role of blood-based biomarkers in guiding the acute management of patients with established traumatic brain injury is unclear. We sought to determine whether concentrations of glial fibrillary acid protein (GFAP) or ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) on hospital day 1 are associated with intracranial pressure (ICP) and therapeutic intensity level (TIL).

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury data set, including patients age 17 years and older with traumatic brain injury and invasive ICP monitoring, excluding those undergoing decompressive craniectomy on admission. Patients were stratified into biomarker quartiles, and the relationships with ICP and TIL were analyzed descriptively. Multivariable linear regressions were performed to test the hypothesis that GFAP and UCH-L1 concentrations were independently associated with ICP and TIL after adjusting for a priori defined covariates.

RESULTS: Two hundred twenty-nine patients with a median age of 39 years (IQR 26-56) were included. Geometric mean concentrations for GFAP and UCH-L1 were 4423 and 989 pg/mL, respectively. Patients in the lowest GFAP quartile had a median of 7.3% of ICP readings >22 mm Hg vs 23.2% in the highest quartile (P < .001); secondary decompressive craniectomy was performed in 16% of the lowest quartile, compared with 39% of the highest quartile (P = .008). After adjusting for covariates, GFAP was significantly associated with ICP burden (B = 8.05, P = .014) and median TIL over 5 days (B = 1.65, P = .009). No significant relationship was seen for UCH-L1.

CONCLUSION: Day 1 blood concentration of GFAP is associated with elevated ICP and may be a useful adjunct when risk-stratifying patients for intracranial hypertension.

item.title: Severity and resource utilisation among trauma patients undergoing trauma team activation in four Danish trauma units: a prospective cohort study.
item.description:
Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Prehospital, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Møller TP, Ipsen EØ, Thiele-Nygaard AE et al.

BACKGROUND: Evidence on trauma epidemiology and outcomes largely originates from major trauma centres, while data from regional trauma units remain limited. The aim of this study was to describe the epidemiology, management, and outcomes of patients undergoing trauma team activation in the trauma units of Region Zealand, Denmark.

METHODS: We conducted a prospective multicentre observational study across four regional trauma units in Region Zealand, Denmark, between 1 March 2024 and 28 February 2025. All consecutive patients undergoing trauma team activation were included. Data included demographics, injury mechanisms, injury severity, in-hospital management, and mortality. Analyses were descriptive.

RESULTS: A total of 1611 patients were included. Median age was 38 years [IQR 20-58], and 60.5% were male. The most common injury mechanisms were traffic-related injuries (53%), falls (22%), and equestrian-related accidents (13%). Median Injury Severity Score was 1 [IQR 0-5] and 94% had Injury Severity Score < 16. Secondary transfer to a major trauma centre occurred in 3.8% of cases, and 90-day mortality was 2.6%. Trauma admissions occurred predominantly outside regular daytime workflow, with a peak in the late afternoon and early evening. Median TTA duration was 58 minutes [IQR 43-76] and CT imaging was performed in 86.7% of cases. Following trauma team activation, 55.2% of patients were discharged directly and 4.6% required intensive care unit admission.

CONCLUSIONS: Most patients undergoing trauma team activation in regional trauma units had minor injuries, were discharged directly from the emergency department, and infrequently required intensive care unit admission or secondary transfer. Despite this, trauma team activation had a median duration around one hour and showed marked diurnal variation, with a peak in the late afternoon and early evening when staffing and clinical resources are typically more limited. These findings highlight opportunities to optimise trauma team activation criteria and organisational structures to better align resource utilisation with patient acuity.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

item.title: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU.
item.description:
Crit Care | Tier 2 Filtered [Cardiac Arrest] [weak match]
Pavez N, Fernández P, Ferrés M et al.

Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) due to Andes virus (ANDV) is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care. This article addresses eleven practical questions on ICU management, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system. The recommendations cover early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA-ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence. Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival relies on early suspicion, physiology-guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO-capable centres when severe cardiopulmonary failure develops.

Full text via DOI

item.title: Influencing factors of the long-term predictive accuracy of the ocular trauma score.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Penetrating] [strong match]
Li W, Fan N, Mei Z et al.

PURPOSE: To evaluate the performance of the Ocular Trauma Score (OTS) in predicting long-term visual outcomes after mechanical ocular trauma and to identify the key factors influencing its accuracy.

METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled 106 patients with mechanical ocular trauma, with a median follow-up of 14 months. Retrieved variables included demographic characteristics and clinical data after the injury. The distribution of final best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was compared between the actual outcomes and the OTS-predicted outcomes. A weighted average predicted BCVA was calculated based on the BCVA probability distribution for each OTS category to classify patients into Better (actual BCVA better than OTS predicted) and Non-Better groups. Factors associated with OTS prediction discrepancies were identified using univariate analyses. Multivariable Firth logistic regression with bootstrap internal validation was performed to identify factors independently associated with better-than-predicted outcomes.

RESULTS: The OTS demonstrated a clear severity-dependent predictive pattern. Predictive accuracy was highest for mild injuries (OTS category 5) but showed a systematic pessimistic bias in severe injuries (OTS category 1), overestimating poor outcomes (NLP) and underestimating recovery potential (BCVA grades 3-5). For intermediate injuries (OTS categories 2-3), the likelihood of achieving moderate vision (20/200-20/50) was underestimated. Multiple surgeries were associated with better-than-predicted outcomes in the univariate analysis (p = 0.021). In the multivariable analysis, endophthalmitis (odds ratio [OR] = 2.95, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.08-8.29, p = 0.034) and penetrating injury (OR = 3.71, 95% CI: 1.17-12.94, p = 0.026) were independently associated with better-than-predicted outcomes, whereas initial BCVA grade 2, despite a significant univariate association, did not retain statistical significance after adjustment (OR = 2.01, 95% CI: 0.79-5.10, p = 0.144).

CONCLUSION: The OTS remains a useful prognostic tool but demonstrates limited accuracy in severe mechanical ocular trauma. Endophthalmitis and penetrating injury were identified as independent modifiers, while initial BCVA grade 2 and multiple surgeries were associated with better-than-predicted outcomes in the univariate analysis. Contextualising its predictions with contemporary surgical factors and clinical modifiers may improve the individualised application of the OTS.

item.title: Focus Where It Matters: Design and Implementation of a Physiology-Based Care Pathway for Traumatic Shock.
item.description:
Emerg Med Australas | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Haemorrhage, Prehospital, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Noonan M, Mathew J, Hendel S et al.

OBJECTIVE: Traumatic shock lacks a consensus definition, and in blunt-predominant systems its causes are heterogeneous. Simple physiological parameters remain the most universally available basis for early recognition. We describe the design and staged implementation of a physiology-based care pathway for traumatic shock and evaluate its implementation through staff experience.

METHODS: Single-centre quality-improvement and implementation project at an Australian Level 1 trauma centre, reported per SQUIRE 2.0. The pathway comprised physiology-based activation (systolic blood pressure ≤ 90 mmHg, shock index > 1, prehospital blood or senior clinician concern), structured pre-arrival preparation, trauma bay and equipment standardisation, task-based team roles, prioritised life-saving interventions and senior-led disposition, supported by simulation and embedded quality improvement. Components were implemented between June and November 2022. Evaluation comprised pre-intervention (2021) and post-implementation (2025) staff surveys, summarised as top-box favourability, with cross-sectional characterisation of the shocked cohort. Clinical effectiveness was not assessed.

RESULTS: Of 3667 major trauma patients, 324 (8.8%) met shocked trauma criteria; these patients were younger, more severely injured and had markedly higher mortality (emergency department death 6.8% vs. 0.4%). Favourable ratings of trauma bay equipment and environment rose from approximately one-quarter to 87.0%. Post-implementation, staff reported high favourability for timely life-saving interventions (88.9%), pathway embedding (85.2%) and role confidence (86.5%). Leadership clarity, communication and reliable debriefing did not improve and were identified as ongoing targets.

CONCLUSIONS: A physiology-based traumatic shock pathway was feasibly implemented and embedded, with high staff-reported readiness and clear targets for refinement. Effectiveness remains to be established.

INTRODUCTION: Secondary procedures after lumbopelvic fixation (LPF) include planned implant removal, removal for symptoms and revision for complications. Their differing indications, together with limited comparative evidence, complicate counselling and surgical planning.

METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched to May 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420251036375) for comparative and single-arm studies (≥10 LPF patients). High-energy injuries and fragility fractures were considered separately. Random-effects models summarised complications, unplanned revision, implant removal and within-study comparisons of surgical approaches and fixation strategies.

RESULTS: Twenty-five studies were included (22 high-energy, 3 fragility). Across 19 high-energy LPF cohorts (564 patients), pooled surgical-site infection was 9.3% (95% CI 6.1-14.1), implant loosening or failure was 5.3%, nonunion occurred in 4 of 389 patients (1.0%) and loss of reduction in 2 of 355. Pooled unplanned revision was 11.9% (95% CI 8.7-16.0; prediction interval 5.3-24.3), most often for infection or wound complications. Implant removal was 79.0% in routine-removal series and 17.3% in selective-removal series. Four studies compared minimally invasive and open LPF. Pooling three studies showed less blood loss with minimally invasive LPF (mean difference -271 mL, 95% CI -367 to -175) and shorter operative time (-51 min, -97 to -5); the operative-time association did not persist with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Infection (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.09-1.83) and revision (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.09-1.43) estimates were inconclusive. Four cohorts comparing LPF with posterior pelvic-ring fixation alone reported higher odds of revision after LPF (OR 3.96, 95% CI 1.63-9.60), with substantial potential for confounding by indication. Certainty was very low.

CONCLUSIONS: Nonunion and loss of reduction were infrequent after LPF, while unplanned revision most often involved infection or wound complications. Implant removal varied with institutional policy and warrants separate counselling. Minimally invasive LPF was associated with less blood loss, but comparative evidence remains insufficient to establish lower complication rates, equivalent mechanical outcomes or superiority of either fixation strategy.

item.title: Impact of sarcopenic obesity phenotype on long-term survival in geriatric trauma: A nationwide cohort study using weight-adjusted waist index.
item.description:

BACKGROUND: As the global population ages, identifying effective prognostic markers for elderly trauma patients has become crucial. While Body Mass Index (BMI) is commonly used, its utility is limited by the "obesity paradox," failing to differentiate between muscle and fat. This study aimed to evaluate the Weight-Adjusted Waist Index (WWI), a surrogate marker for sarcopenic obesity, as a predictor of 20-year mortality following heavy trauma in the elderly.

METHODS: We analyzed a nationwide cohort of 18,366 elderly patients (age≧65) from the National Health Insurance Service-National Sample Cohort (NHIS-NSC) who experienced heavy trauma (hospitalization, surgery, or ICU admission) between 2002 and 2022. Patients were categorized into WWI tertiles. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for 20-year mortality, adjusting for demographics, lifestyle factors, comorbidities, and laboratory findings.

RESULTS: During the 20-year follow-up, the highest WWI tertile (T3) was associated with significantly higher mortality compared to the lowest tertile (T1). In the fully adjusted model, the HR for 20-year mortality in the T3 group was 1.72 (95% CI 1.55-1.91). Notably, the risk was more pronounced in obese patients (BMI≧25 kg/m2, HR 2.15) and those with low physical activity. Furthermore, high WWI was associated with a higher prevalence of hip and femur fractures (26.0% vs. 15.0%) and prolonged ICU stays.

CONCLUSIONS: WWI is a superior and independent predictor of long-term mortality compared to BMI in elderly trauma patients. By effectively identifying the high-risk sarcopenic obesity phenotype, WWI provides a practical and powerful tool for risk stratification in geriatric trauma management.

BACKGROUND: Delayed diagnosis of hollow viscus injury (HVI) from blunt trauma (BT) carries increased morbidity. An HVI prediction tool (HVI Score), incorporating vital signs, physical examination, and computed tomography (CT) findings has been validated in patients injured by motor vehicle collision (MVC) with an abdominal seatbelt sign. This study investigated the HVI Score performance in patients with non-MVC blunt trauma.

METHODS: This retrospective single-center study conducted between 2020 and 2024 included adult (>18-years-old) patients sustaining non-MVC BT who underwent CT imaging of the abdomen/pelvis prior to any abdominal operation. The primary outcome was operatively confirmed HVI. HVI Score model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve and by calibration (ratio of observed to expected events, calibration-in-the-large, and calibration slope).

RESULTS: Of 752 non-MVC BT patients admitted, 19 (2.5%) were high-risk (scores >10), 105 (14.0%) moderate-risk (scores 6-9), and 628 (83.5%) low-risk (scores <5), with 19 (2.5%) having an HVI. The high-risk cohort had increased rates of abdominal tenderness (36.8% vs. 27.6% vs. 12.1%) as well as increased CT findings of free fluid (100.0% vs. 89.5% vs. 6.1%), soft tissue contusion (73.7% vs. 46.7% vs. 28.8%), mesenteric stranding (36.8% vs. 21.0% vs.7.6%), mesenteric hematoma (42.1% vs. 13.3% vs. 7.8%), bowel wall thickening (47.4% vs. 5.7% vs. 3.3%), and pneumoperitoneum (26.3% vs. 1.9% vs. 0.0%) compared to moderate and low-risk patients (all p < 0.001). The HVI Score achieved an AUROC of 0.96 (CI 0.94-0.98). Observed events numbered 19 against 26 expected (observed-to-expected ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.47-1.15), with a calibration slope of 0.96 (95% CI 0.64-1.28). At the low-risk threshold, sensitivity and NPV were both 100%; at the high-risk threshold, specificity was 99% and PPV 47%.

CONCLUSION: The HVI Score, which was originally validated for MVC patients with a seatbelt sign, had excellent performance in predicting HVI among patients with non-MVC BT.

SOCIAL MEDIA SUMMARY: The Hollow Viscus Injury (HVI) prediction score has excellent performance in predicting HVI among patients with non-MVC blunt abdominal trauma, thus extending its utility to all blunt trauma patients.

BACKGROUND: Pickleball participation continues to surge, with many recreational tennis players transitioning to the sport due to perceived ease of play and social appeal. The aim of this study was to compare 11-year injury patterns between patients presenting to the Emergency Department (ED) for pickleball and tennis injuries.

HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that (1) pickleball-related ED visits would increase over time while tennis-related visits would remain stable or decrease; (2) injury patterns would differ between sports by anatomical site, diagnosis, and mechanism; and (3) older adults would account for a higher proportion of fall-related injuries requiring hospital admission.

STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective comparative epidemiologic study LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III METHODS: National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) data between 2014 and 2024 were sorted for pickleball (product code 3235) and tennis (product code 3284). Cases were manually reviewed to confirm sport participation and exclude non-musculoskeletal injuries. Anatomical site, diagnosis, injury mechanism, treatment disposition, and date of ED visit were extracted. Group comparisons used t-tests and chi-square tests, and linear regression evaluated annual trends.

RESULTS: A total of 4141 cases were included (pickleball n = 1442; National Estimates (NE) 80,553; tennis n = 2699; NE 110,480). Pickleball-related ED visits increased over time, while tennis-related visits remained stable. Pickleball players were older than tennis players (60.1 (SD 16.7) yr vs. 40.9 (SD 23.3) yr; p < 0.01), with individuals ≥ 65 years accounting for 52.1% of pickleball-related injuries. Wrist injuries were the most common in pickleball (17.0%) and ankle injuries were most common in tennis (18.3%). Fractures were more frequent in pickleball (43.1%), while sprains/strains were more common in tennis (46.4%, p < 0.01). Falls were the leading mechanism in both sports (Pickleball 52.2%, Tennis 33.8%). Pickleball injuries occurred most frequently in the Winter (30.3%) while tennis injuries occurred most frequently in Summer (29.1%). Hospital admissions were more frequent for pickleball players (7.8% vs 3.9%).

CONCLUSIONS: The rapid rise in pickleball-related injuries necessitates proactive efforts in education, conditioning, and injury prevention to safeguard participants, particularly older adults.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: As participation in pickleball grows, especially among older adults, targeted conditioning, emphasizing neuromuscular control and safety education may help reduce injury rates.

Zhang T, Cai Q, Liang B et al.

PURPOSE: To systematically describe the epidemiological characteristics of rib fractures in South China and compare the clinical characteristics, hospital stay, and total costs between patients receiving conservative versus surgical treatment, thereby providing evidence‑based support for clinical decision‑making and public health prevention.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed on 4085 hospitalized patients with rib fractures admitted to the Fifth Affiliated Hospital of Southern Medical University between January 2014 and December 2023. Data on gender, age, injury mechanism, fracture type, complications, blood group, and occupational distribution were collected. A subgroup analysis comparing conservative (n = 586) versus surgical treatment (n = 137) was conducted among 723 patients admitted between January 2021 and December 2023. Propensity score matching was used to balance baseline characteristics between the two groups, and differences in hospital stay, total costs, and injury mechanisms were compared.

RESULTS: (1) Epidemiological characteristics: Of the 4085 patients, 68.13% (2783/4085) were male, and the 41-60 year age group accounted for the highest proportion (50.35%). Autumn and winter were the peak seasons for injury (54.71%). Traffic accidents were the leading cause of injury (51.18%), followed by falls (21.82%) and height‑related falls (19.13%). Multiple fractures predominated (75.52%). The most common complication was pulmonary contusion (45.14%), followed by traumatic pneumothorax/hemothorax/hemopneumothorax/pleural effusion (40.02%). Among occupations, freelancers were the largest group (34.37%), followed by farmers (23.18%). Blood group O was the most prevalent (42.15%), while blood group B was the least common (5.55%, P < 0.001), suggesting that blood group O may be a potential risk factor for rib fractures. (2) Comparison of treatment modalities: The conservative group had a significantly shorter hospital stay than the surgical group [3 (2-6) days vs. 17 (13-26) days, P < 0.001] and significantly lower total costs [5879 (2570-8877) RMB vs. 69,588 (54,499-89,845) RMB, P < 0.001]. The distribution of injury mechanisms differed significantly between the two groups (P < 0.001): the conservative group was mainly injured by falls/slips (44.4%), whereas the surgical group was mainly injured by height‑related falls/ground‑level falls (30.7%). The proportion of concomitant hemopneumothorax was higher in the surgical group than in the conservative group (21.9% vs. 3.4%, P < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: Based on a large sample of 4085 cases, this study is the first to systematically delineate the full epidemiological profile of rib fractures in South China, with a sample size more than ten times larger than the previous largest regional report. The results indicate that middle‑aged males, freelancers, and farmers are high‑risk populations, with traffic accidents and multiple fractures being predominant, and a unique autumn peak seasonal pattern in South China is reported for the first time. Treatment strategies should be tailored according to injury mechanism and fracture severity. The novel association between blood group O and increased rib fracture risk, reported here for the first time, provides a new perspective for precision prevention; the potential mechanism may involve impaired hemostatic response due to lower baseline levels of von Willebrand factor and factor VIII in individuals with blood group O.

BACKGROUND: Coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus exhibit diverse fracture-extension patterns that are not fully characterized by conventional classification systems. The clinical significance of fracture extension into the medial or lateral column remains incompletely understood. This study investigated fracture-extension patterns beyond the conventional Dubberley classification and evaluated their associations with clinical outcomes and bone-related complications.

METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study included surgically treated coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus with a minimum follow-up of 12 months at four affiliated institutions between 2012 and 2024. Fractures were classified using the AO/OTA and Dubberley systems. Computed tomography (CT) images were reviewed to assess medial trochlear involvement, lateral column involvement without posterior condylar comminution, and isolated trochlear fractures. Clinical outcomes included elbow range of motion (flexion, extension, and arc of motion) and postoperative complications. Univariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with bone-related complications.

In univariate logistic regression analysis, medial trochlear involvement was significantly associated with bone-related complications (odds ratio, 12.5; 95% confidence interval, 1.69-92.3; P = 0.013). Neither the AO/OTA nor the Dubberley classification was significantly associated with bone-related complications.

CONCLUSIONS: Medial trochlear involvement was significantly associated with greater loss of elbow extension and bone-related complications at final follow-up in coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus. BACKGROUND: Admission information can help describe surgical treatment and subsequent functional outcomes following traumatic brain injury (TBI). We developed interpretable machine learning models to address these two tasks.

METHODS: This retrospective study included 673 adults evaluated at a single center between December 2018 and December 2023. Outcomes recorded were neurosurgical intervention and six-month Glasgow Outcome Scale status, dichotomized as favorable (scores 4-5) or unfavorable (scores 1-3). Patients were randomly allocated to training and internal validation sets in a 7:3 ratio. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used to select predictors for the XGBoost and random forest models. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, along with classification and prediction error metrics, was employed for model evaluation. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were used to interpret model predictions.

The reported validation accuracy for XGBoost was 87.56% for predicting functional outcomes and 95.02% for surgical interventions. Validation Brier scores were 0.083 and 0.035, respectively. Interpretation of threshold-dependent measures is limited by class imbalance and incomplete specification of outcome coding.

CONCLUSION: The models combined routinely collected admission variables to characterize the treatment received and functional outcomes in a selected traumatic brain injury (TBI) cohort. These findings require confirmation through analysis replication and independent validation before they can be applied clinically.

item.title: Articular compliance and tolerance to residual incongruity after intra-articular fracture: A hypothesis-driven narrative review.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]

BACKGROUND: Residual articular incongruity after intra-articular fracture is widely held to cause post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA), yet tolerance of a given step-off differs between joints and between regions of the same joint. Reduction targets are nonetheless expressed as uniform millimetre thresholds, and no tissue-level mechanism has been offered for the variation.

HYPOTHESIS: The compliance of the osteochondral unit - cartilage thickness, cartilage material properties and subchondral bone stiffness together - modulates tolerance of residual incongruity, and incongruity is more informatively expressed relative to local cartilage thickness than in absolute millimetres.

METHODS: Narrative review with a documented search of PubMed/MEDLINE (inception to 14 October 2026) covering cartilage and subchondral properties of opposing surfaces, experimental and computational studies of articular incongruity, and clinical studies relating residual displacement to outcome. Four searches returned 3928 records, 3579 after deduplication; 54 sources informed the synthesis. This is not a systematic review; reporting follows SANRA.

FINDINGS: Small, localised contact-stress elevations appear tolerable; step-offs remodel less completely as their height increases; and cumulative contact-stress exposure above a threshold predicts PTOA after tibial plafond fracture. Opposing surfaces differ measurably in cartilage thickness, modulus and subchondral bone thickness, but the direction of the difference reverses between joints and between regions of one joint, so curvature is not a usable proxy for compliance. Clinically, the acetabulum and tibial plafond appear least tolerant, the meniscus-covered tibial plateau more tolerant, and distal radius incongruity predicts radiographic arthrosis more strongly than functional loss.

CONCLUSIONS: The evidence is consistent with, but does not establish, a contribution of osteochondral compliance; joint-level factors confound the clinical data. We set out a Compliance Framework defining measurable determinants, propose relative incongruity as a testable metric, and state four falsifiable predictions with the designs that would test them. Current joint-specific reduction standards should guide practice until those predictions are tested.

BACKGROUND: Cricket is one of the most widely played sports worldwide and carries a significant burden of musculoskeletal injuries, particularly among fast bowlers. Over the past four decades, research in cricket injury epidemiology, biomechanics, workload monitoring, and surveillance has expanded substantially.

Workload spikes were strongly associated with increased injury risk, establishing load monitoring as a central preventive strategy. OBJECTIVES: When infusion pumps are unavailable in the prehospital setting, clinicians must estimate fluid flow by counting drops in a drip chamber. We aimed to assess the accuracy and precision of gravity-driven infusions and to estimate the magnitude of inaccuracy and imprecision attributable to human and non-human factors.

METHODS: We recruited 55 paramedics to participate in structured, experimental, simulated study under controlled laboratory conditions, in which each participant set nine drip rates as accurately as possible on a standardized setup. Measurements of flow were made visually (drip rate) and volumetrically (delivered fluid). Volumetric measurements were used to represent overall error, visual measurements were used to represent human error, and the difference was used to represent non-human error. We measured accuracy (percentage error) and precision (mean absolute deviation) using the natural log of error factor to represent the multiplicative decomposition of human and non-human error additively. Mixed effect models were used to assess accuracy and precision across targeted drip rates.

RESULTS: Inaccuracy and imprecision varied by targeted drip rate. Overall inaccuracy ranged from -45.3% (95%CI, -52.7% to -36.8%) to 5.8% (95%CI, -8.5% to 22.3%). Human inaccuracy ranged from -38.8% (95%CI, -46.0% to -30.8%) to 44.1% (95%CI, 27.1% to 63.4%). Non-human inaccuracy ranged from -26.7% (95%CI, -30.1% to -23.2%) to -6.8% (95%CI -11.1% to -2.3%). Imprecision was primarily driven by human factors. The degree of human variation between trial participants ranged from 24.2% (95%CI, 15.3% to 33.7%) to 43.7% (95%CI, 33.4% to 54.9%) across targeted rates. The targeted drip rate of 1gtt/s was more accurate than the pool of all other targeted rates (absolute error 31.1% versus 48.5%). Targeted drip rates of whole numbers were more accurate than targeted drip rates of fractional numbers (absolute error 40.7% versus 54.1%). Targeted drip rates below 1gtt/s were more accurate than rates above 1gtt/s (absolute error 35.3% versus 63.1%).

CONCLUSIONS: Gravity-driven fluid delivery exhibits inaccuracy and imprecision, which varies by targeted rate. While potentially modifiable human factors may improve the accuracy of this technique, non-human error contributes substantially to inaccuracy. There is a need to assess whether this inaccuracy and imprecision adversely affect patient outcomes.

Spine and peripheral nerve (5227 devices) and stereotactic and functional (1378) dominated volume and number of new market entries, while cerebrospinal fluid disorders (n = 149) and cranial trauma (n = 111) had fewer approvals. Cerebrovascular and endovascular (95.5%) and cranial trauma (200.0%) showed the largest growth rates, while cerebrospinal fluid disorders (-54.2%) and general cranial surgery (-34.5%) declined over time. Mean approval time varied by subspecialty (P < .001), the shortest for spine and peripheral nerve (119.0 ± 102.7 days) and the longest for stereotactic and functional (158.7 ± 121.5 days). Approval or clearance times were strongly influenced by regulatory pathway and device class (both P < .001), with Premarket Approval devices (584.8 ± 323.3 days) the longest. Mature companies achieved faster approvals compared with startups (114.9 ± 97.0 vs 174.5 ± 133.9 days, P < .001).

CONCLUSION: Neurosurgical device output has more than doubled, but volume concentrates where predicates are rich and reimbursement established, not where clinical need or novelty is the greatest. Pathway architecture, device complexity, and sponsor experience influence approval efficiency more than novelty.

item.title: Coagulopathy and anticoagulation management in adult ECPR patients.
item.description:
Crit Care | Tier 2 Filtered [Cardiac Arrest] [strong match]
Rajsic S, Lansink-Hartgring AO, Swol J et al.

Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a lifesaving strategy for refractory cardiac arrest, restoring systemic perfusion when conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation fails. However, ECPR profoundly disrupts haemostasis, driven by the combined effects of whole-body ischaemia-reperfusion injury, systemic inflammation, endothelial activation, platelet dysfunction, and blood contact with extracorporeal surfaces. Together, these processes create a highly dynamic and unstable thromboinflammatory milieu, marked by the simultaneous risk of thrombosis and life-threatening bleeding. Systemic anticoagulation is required to maintain circuit patency and prevent thromboembolic complications, yet optimal strategies remain uncertain. Haemostasis during ECPR is highly dynamic, shaped by the underlying aetiology of cardiac arrest, patient-specific characteristics, and circuit-related factors. This complexity underscores the limitations of fixed anticoagulation targets and the need for individualized, context-sensitive management guided by continuous clinical and laboratory assessment. Despite the increasing global adoption of ECPR, high-quality evidence to guide anticoagulation practices remains scarce. Current strategies are largely extrapolated from other extracorporeal life support populations, contributing to substantial inter-centre variability. This review synthesizes the available evidence on coagulopathy and anticoagulation in adult patients receiving ECPR and discusses emerging approaches to monitoring and anticoagulation management.

item.title: Assessing Swedish guidelines for prehospital bleeding control: a cross-sectional appraisal using AGREE II.
item.description:
Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Prehospital] [strong match]
Gifting W, Johansson L, Andersson Hagiwara M et al.

BACKGROUND: High-quality clinical practice guidelines are essential for safe and consistent prehospital bleeding control, particularly in settings with variable geography and transport times. This study appraised the methodological quality of Swedish regional prehospital guidelines for traumatic external haemorrhage using the AGREE II instrument.

METHODS: This cross-sectional study included clinical practice guidelines requested from all 21 Swedish healthcare regions. Guideline quality was assessed independently by two appraisers using AGREE II, which evaluates 23 items across six domains. Domain scores were calculated as percentages of the maximum possible score.

RESULTS: Complete responses were obtained from 15 of 21 regions. Overall methodological quality was low across the included guidelines. The highest median domain score was observed for clarity of presentation, whereas rigour of development, stakeholder involvement, applicability, and editorial independence scored poorly. Most guidelines lacked explicit descriptions of evidence search strategies, criteria for selecting evidence, links between recommendations and supporting evidence, update procedures, and declarations of editorial independence.

CONCLUSIONS: Swedish regional prehospital guidelines for traumatic external bleeding control showed limited methodological quality when assessed using AGREE II. Future guideline development should prioritise transparent evidence linkage, multidisciplinary stakeholder involvement, clear implementation considerations, scheduled updating, and adaptation to regional differences in transport and evacuation times.

item.title: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden.
item.description:
Crit Care | Tier 2 Filtered [Prehospital] [weak match]
Lileikyte G, Marinho LL, Lu Y et al.

INTRODUCTION: The optimal temperature target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain, as major randomized trials have not demonstrated a clear benefit of lower-target hypothermia compared with normothermia. Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0-37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission.

METHODS: This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4-6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials' primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56-73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from - 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest (p = 0.99), and from - 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome.

CONCLUSIONS: Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

item.title: Current models of emergency general surgery care delivery in Manitoba, Canada: a cross-sectional survey.
item.description:
World J Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [weak match]
Garland C, Aldekhayel M, Garland A et al.

BACKGROUND: Emergency general surgery conditions result in disproportionately high rates of morbidity and mortality. Despite this, little is known about the resources available for related care in Canadian hospitals. Our aim was to describe the resources and structures dedicated to emergency general surgery in Manitoba, Canada.

METHODOLOGY: We developed a survey to examine institutional capabilities in providing emergency general surgical care. The survey was developed over three iterations using a modified Delphi technique and was then reviewed separately by community surgeons to ensure broad applicability. A cross-sectional survey of representatives at each of the fourteen hospitals reported to offer emergency general surgery care in Manitoba was performed in two iterations between March and December 2023. Findings were examined descriptively and stratified between tertiary, urban, and rural centres. Our aim was to describe the resources and structures in place for providing related care, including the proportion of hospitals with a dedicated emergency general surgery care model.

RESULTS: After exclusions and non-responses, we examined the resources and capabilities of nine institutions. Two tertiary, two urban community, and five rural community centres were evaluated. Of these institutions, 4/9 (44.4%) had an emergency general surgery model of care, including one rural centre. There was a large degree of variation in operative resources, specialty services, and physician learners between centre types. Allied health professionals were more consistently available across hospitals. Our survey results identified several pertinent gaps in care, including a lack of shared treatment protocols, transfer agreements, and quality improvement measures, even at large tertiary centres.

CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates a pressing need for collaboration between centres and involvement in quality improvement amongst practitioners to meet standards of care in emergency general surgery. The results also show that important aspects of emergency general surgical care can be quantified with our survey and will serve as the basis for expanding this to a country-wide study.

item.title: Impact of the provider-in-triage model on computed tomography and ultrasound imaging in renal colic.
item.description:
Am J Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [Imaging] [weak match]
Thom C, Mullins C, Spirek B et al.

INTRODUCTION: Physician-in-Triage (PIT) models may influence diagnostic imaging decisions in the emergency department (ED). We evaluated the association between PIT exposure and imaging utilization among patients with renal colic and examined the influence of physician ultrasound training on imaging selection.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with an ED diagnosis of renal colic at a single tertiary ED from January 2024 through December 2025. A prespecified lower-risk subgroup included patients aged <51 years with prior nephrolithiasis, no infection, and normal creatinine. The primary exposure was PIT evaluation. Outcomes included computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis (CTAP), point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), and radiology-performed renal ultrasound (RUS) utilization. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between PIT exposure and each imaging outcome after adjustment for age, gender, emergency severity index, admission, and race.

RESULTS: Of 1041 patients, 596 (57.3%) were exposed to PIT. CTAP utilization was higher among PIT-exposed patients than non-PIT patients (72.9% vs 66.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.40, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07-1.85). PIT exposure was associated with lower POCUS utilization (10.3% vs 18.6%; aOR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34-0.70), while RUS utilization was similar (10.1% vs 9.0%; aOR 1.17, 95% CI 0.76-1.79). Overall ultrasound utilization (POCUS or RUS) was also lower among PIT-exposed patients (20.1% vs 26.7%; aOR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51-0.93). In the lower-risk subgroup, PIT exposure remained associated with greater CTAP utilization (63.6% vs 48.1%, p = 0.028) and lower POCUS utilization (14.4% vs 30.4%, p = 0.008). Ultrasound-trained attendings used CTAP less frequently than non-ultrasound-trained attendings (57.8% vs 71.8%; aOR for non-ultrasound-trained physicians 1.86, 95% CI 1.18-2.93).

CONCLUSION: PIT exposure was associated with greater CTAP and lower ultrasound utilization in patients with renal colic, including among a prespecified lower-risk cohort. Ultrasound-trained physicians used ultrasound more frequently and CTAP less frequently in renal colic patients.

item.title: Long-Term Survival Following Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Two-Center Five-Year Analysis.
item.description:
Resuscitation | Tier 2 Filtered [Cardiac Arrest] [weak match]
Alexy T, Beery J, Gottula AL et al.

Randomized trials have shown short-term benefit of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but the long-term durability of survival and neurological recovery after hospital discharge remains poorly defined. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory VT/VF OHCA from two academic centers (University of Minnesota, USA, and Charles University, Prague) from January 2013 through December 2022. The primary outcome was 5-year survival. Secondary outcomes included neurological status by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) and associations of age and discharge disposition with long-term outcomes. Among 728 patients treated with ECPR, 211 (29.0%) survived to discharge; 138 from Minnesota and 73 from Prague. Median follow-up was 3.9 years; 68 patients (32%) completed 5 years. No patients were lost to follow-up. Among hospital survivors, 76.9% and 67.2% were alive at 1 and 5 years, respectively, with most deaths occurring within 90 days of discharge. CPC 1-2 was present in 78.7% at discharge and remained high among survivors beyond 1 year (93.4%-94.2%). Five-year survival declined by age from 91.6% for those between 18-39 years to 52.9% for >70 years. Discharge disposition also strongly stratified long-term prognosis. Among patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA, long-term survival was substantial, with approximately two-thirds alive at 5 years with favorable CPC in most. Younger age and discharge home or to acute rehabilitation identified subgroups with particularly favorable prognosis. These findings support the long-term durability of benefit among selected patients treated within established ECPR systems of care.

item.description:

BACKGROUND: Pediatric flexor tendon injuries are rare but potentially devastating. Due to low incidence, optimal perioperative management remains poorly defined, and evidence is scarce. This study evaluates the injury characteristics, surgical treatment, age-specific functional outcomes, and challenges in this population.

METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted on 79 pediatric patients (mean age 6.84 ± 4.27 years; 67.1% male) who underwent surgical repair for flexor tendon lacerations between 2010 and 2023. Outcomes were assessed using Total Active Motion (TAM), Strickland score, grip/pinch strength, Semmes-Weinstein monofilament, two-point discrimination, and QuickDASH questionnaire, with a mean follow-up of 59.9 ± 32.8 months.

RESULTS: Zone 2 was the most common injury site (45.6%), with glass being the predominant mechanism (67.1%). Nerve injury was present in 35.4% of cases. Overall, good/excellent results were achieved in 81.9% (TAM) and 89.0% (Strickland) of patients. The 0-5 years age group had significantly lower Strickland scores than the 6-12 years group (74.28% vs. 82.9%, p < 0.05). Zone 5 injuries demonstrated significantly better outcomes than Zone 2 and 3 (p < 0.001). The overall complication rate was low (5.1%), with a rerupture rate of 2.5%.

CONCLUSION: Pediatric flexor tendon repairs yield favorable functional outcomes with low complication rates. Age-related differences in functional outcomes should be interpreted cautiously because of developmental differences in patient cooperation and age-dependent rehabilitation strategies. Concomitant nerve injury was associated with poorer functional outcomes. The modified Kessler technique remains a reliable repair method.

INTRODUCTION: The objective of this study was to describe the Limb Preservation and Optimization Center's (LPOC) components and mechanisms in treating catastrophic extremity injuries and report the initial patient demographics, indications, and outcomes using data from an established registry.

METHODS: A retrospective observational study was performed including all patients entered in the LPOC registry since January 1, 2014. Patient demographics, injury types and treatments, and outcomes, including functional outcomes. Descriptive statistics were calculated to determine proportions, means, standard deviations, and ranges.

RESULTS: 992 patients were included with a mean final follow-up of 20.5 months (SD:22.1, range 0-114); 178 (17.9%) underwent an amputation. Of those who reported RTW, 164 patients (71.6%) reporting RTW at full capacity. Lower extremity injuries were most common (74.9%). Demographic, health insurance, living setting, and presentation variables were similar among LPOC patients. Fractures and soft tissue injuries predominated across all injury categories with fracture fixation and wound coverage treatments most common. Upper extremity joint injuries and all types of combined injuries were associated with the highest reoperation rates. Treatment failure rates ranged from 11% to 100% with fracture and bone-related injuries being associated with the most favorable outcomes across categories.

DISCUSSION: Fractures and soft tissue injuries were the primary types of problems affecting all patients utilizing the LPOC. Fracture fixation and wound coverage treatments were the most performed procedures. Return to the operating room to address the limb preservation and optimization goal was extremely common across categories such that patients may expect at least 4 reoperations. Patients return to some type of work 75-88%. Treatment failure rates varied from 11% to 100%, with fracture and bone-related injuries being associated with the most favorable outcomes across categories. Overall, the results are encouraging and will help shape care in these patients.

BACKGROUND: Geodemographic factors create divergent clinical patterns between urban and rural settings. Level-II trauma centers are a vital trauma-care infrastructure for both urban and rural communities. This study compares neck trauma patterns, resource utilization, and outcomes at these distinct geodemographic nodes.

METHODS: Retrospective analysis (2014-2024) of neck trauma at an urban center (UC, n = 65) and a rural center (RC, n = 60). Demographics, mechanism, treatments, interventions, and outcomes were analyzed.

RESULTS: RC patients sustained more blunt, transport-related multisystem trauma with higher ISS. UC patients predominantly presented with localized penetrating injuries. Rural patients had higher ICU admission rates, longer ICU stays, more transfers to level-I centers yet underwent fewer operative interventions, invasive airway procedures, and CT angiogrophy.

CONCLUSIONS: There are significant variations in neck trauma between urban and rural level-II trauma centers. An "intervention paradox" exists were rural centers stabilize high-severity blunt trauma for transfer, while urban centers provide definitive care for penetrating wounds. These findings necessitate geodemographically tailored protocols. Understanding geodemographic variations is a critical aspect of optimizing trauma systems.

item.title: Gabapentinoid-opioid co-prescription after long bone fracture fixation is associated with increased 1-year nonunion.
item.description:

PURPOSE: Gabapentinoids are increasingly incorporated into multimodal analgesia after orthopaedic surgery, yet their impact on outcomes following fracture fixation remains unclear. This study evaluated the association between early postoperative gabapentinoid-opioid co-prescription and clinical outcomes after operative fixation of closed long bone fractures.

METHODS: Using TriNetX, we identified opioid-naïve and gabapentinoid-naïve adults undergoing intramedullary or plate-and-screw fixation of isolated closed diaphyseal tibia, humerus, or femur fractures. Patients prescribed gabapentin or pregabalin and opioids within three days after surgery were compared with patients receiving opioids alone. Propensity score matching (1:1) incorporated demographics, medical comorbidities, fracture location, fixation method, mental health disorders, and substance use disorders. Primary outcomes were prolonged (30-90 days) and chronic (90-180 days) postoperative opioid use. Secondary outcomes included 30-day emergency department (ED) visits and readmissions, and 1-year nonunion and reoperation.

RESULTS: After matching, each cohort consisted of approximately 2000 patients (range, 1946-2012). Gabapentinoid-opioid therapy was associated with higher rates of prolonged (21.0% vs 16.1%; RR 1.31; p < 0.001) and chronic (9.8% vs 7.4%; RR 1.33; p = 0.007) postoperative opioid use. Gabapentinoid-opioid therapy was associated with fewer 30-day ED visits (25.1% vs 42.5%; RR 0.59; p < 0.001), while 30-day readmission rates were similar between cohorts (p = 0.174). One-year rates of nonunion (4.3% vs 1.9%; RR 2.21; p < 0.001) and reoperation (7.1% vs 4.2%; RR 1.68; p < 0.001) were significantly higher among patients receiving gabapentinoid-opioid therapy. In a sensitivity analysis that defined the opioid-only cohort based on the absence of gabapentinoid prescriptions during the first 3 postoperative days, rather than the 1-year postoperative medication window used in the primary analysis, the associations with prolonged and chronic opioid use and reoperation were no longer statistically significant, whereas the association with nonunion remained significant (RR 1.62; p = 0.001).

CONCLUSION: Gabapentinoid-opioid therapy was associated with fewer ED visits and higher rates of prolonged and chronic opioid use, nonunion, and reoperation; in sensitivity analysis, ED visits and nonunion remained significant, whereas opioid use and reoperation did not. These findings suggest that potential short-term analgesic benefits may be offset by adverse long-term outcomes, warranting caution and further study of gabapentinoid-opioid prescribing for acute perioperative fracture pain.
