BACKGROUND: Immediate surgical exploration is recommended for suspected hollow viscus injury (HVI) following blunt trauma. However, diagnostic uncertainty can lead to delayed operative management. We aimed to evaluate if delayed bowel resection/repair (DBR), defined as ≥8 hours after emergency department arrival, was independently associated with increased mortality in blunt trauma patients. We also sought to identify risk factors associated with DBR.

METHODS: The Trauma Quality Improvement Program database (2017-2024) was queried for admitted adults with blunt abdominal trauma (abdomen abbreviated injury scale grade ≥2) who underwent bowel resection/repair. Patients who were transferred from another facility or died within 8 hours were excluded. Patients undergoing early bowel resection <8 hours (EBR) were compared with patients undergoing DBR (≥8 h). Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between DBR and mortality, controlling for age, severe head and thoracic injury, intubation within 1 hour of arrival, injury to the small bowel, colon, or rectum, and blood transfusion within 4 hours.

RESULTS: Of 33,728 patients undergoing bowel resection/repair, 16,010 (47.5%) underwent DBR. The DBR cohort had lower rates of small bowel (49.6% vs. 53.9%, p<0.001) and colon (46.7% vs. 49.7%, p<0.001) injuries, but similar rates of rectal injury (4.4% vs. 4.1%, p=0.166). Injuries to the liver (26.8% vs. 20.8%), spleen (28.2% vs. 23.4%), and kidney (12.9% vs. 9.0%) were more frequent in the DBR cohort (all p<0.001). DBR patients had an increased associated risk of mortality (13.0% vs. 8.5%, OR 1.21, 95% CI: 1.12-1.30, p<0.001). Small bowel injury was the only independent factor with decreased associated risk of DBR (OR 0.93, CI: 0.89-0.97, p=0.001).

CONCLUSION: Delayed operative management for blunt HVI occurs more often in patients with solid organ injuries and is independently associated with increased mortality. These findings highlight the importance of early detection and timely surgical management of HVI.

item.title: Hypoxia Paradox in Middle Meningeal Artery Embolization for Chronic Subdural Hematoma: A Mechanistic Framework for Treatment Resistance.
item.description:
Neurosurgery | Tier 2 Filtered [TBI] [strong match]
Shimohigoshi W, Mizutani A, Demura M et al.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The clinical efficacy of middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) in chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH) is increasingly established; yet, recent landmark randomized controlled trials consistently report only a 30% to 50% reduction in recurrence, implying that middle meningeal artery occlusion alone does not fully resolve the pathological microenvironment of the outer hematoma membrane. The mechanistic basis of this incomplete treatment response remains undefined.

METHODS: To develop a mechanistic framework for this clinical paradox, we performed a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses-compliant systematic review. Of 876 records identified across PubMed, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov, 47 underwent full-text review and 18 studies (16 clinical studies and 2 registry records) published through October 2025 were included, integrating clinical outcomes with pathological and molecular insights. A secondary analysis of a publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing data set of normal human dural tissue was performed to map the cellular infrastructure underlying key molecular drivers.

RESULTS: CSDH progression is driven by an interconnected triad of inflammatory infiltration, pathological angiogenesis, and vascular hyperpermeability within the outer hematoma membrane. While MMAE suppresses these pathogenic programs by reducing middle meningeal artery-derived arterial supply, we propose that occlusion-induced ischemic stress may paradoxically stabilize hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, triggering compensatory angiogenesis in cases of incomplete devascularization, a mechanism we formally term the "hypoxia paradox". Secondary single-cell RNA sequencing analysis identified fibroblast-like and endothelial dural populations as the primary cellular platforms for this response, providing a translational cellular basis for the proposed framework.

CONCLUSION: The hypoxia paradox represents a testable mechanistic hypothesis, offering a coherent explanation for heterogeneous MMAE outcomes and generates specific, testable predictions regarding post-MMAE molecular signatures in the outer hematoma membrane. Prospective paired tissue sampling integrated with multimodal molecular analyses is essential to validate this model and advance CSDH management toward individualized, mechanism-guided therapy.

BACKGROUND: The aim of this study was to evaluate biomechanically whether fixation of posterolateral tibial plateau fractures (PLTPFs) through the more accessible modified anterolateral approach and by using a newly designed lateral plate with or without posterior plate extension or supplemental anteroposterior screw fixation, can provide comparable stability to direct posterolateral buttress plating.

METHODS: PLTPFs were simulated on 40 artificial tibiae and subsequently fixed with 5 different plating techniques (n = 8), namely using Variable Angle Locking Compression Plate (VA-LCP) Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (VA Lateral), Variable Angle Optimized Locking Technology (VOLT) Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (VOLT Lateral), VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with Posterolateral Extension (Hug), VOLT Posterolateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (PL), and VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with two anteroposterior parallel 3.5 mm locking screws placed superiorly to the plate's lateral-to-medial rafting locking screws (Jail) using a dedicated guide block. Biomechanical testing was performed under progressively increasing cyclic loading to failure. Interfragmentary movements were monitored via motion tracking.

RESULTS: Fragment displacement and its posterior tilt over the first 40,000 cycles did not differ significantly between Hug, PL, and Jail (all p > 0.999). Hug, PL, and Jail outperformed VA Lateral significantly in terms of fragment displacement over 40,000 cycles (p ≤ 0.004). In addition, Hug was associated with significantly less fragment displacement versus VOLT Lateral (p = 0.018). Posterior fragment tilting over 40,000 cycles was significantly lower in Hug, PL, and Jail versus VA Lateral and VOLT Lateral (p ≤ 0.014). Hug, PL, and Jail demonstrated significantly higher cycles to clinical failure and corresponding loads at clinical failure than VA Lateral and VOLT Lateral (p < 0.001), with no significant differences among Hug, PL, and Jail (p > 0.999). For catastrophic failure, Hug demonstrated significantly higher values than all other groups (p ≤ 0.045).

CONCLUSION: From a biomechanical perspective, VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with Posterolateral Extension and VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate with supplemental jail screw fixation provide fixation stability comparable to VOLT Posterolateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with respect to fragment displacement, posterior tilt, and clinical failure. Whether PLTPFs could be addressed via the more accessible anterolateral approach without compromising the biomechanical stability of fracture fixation remains yet to be clinically validated. Standalone Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (VA-LCP or VOLT) performed inferiorly to their augmented alternatives.

BACKGROUND: Hip fractures represent a growing public health burden. Optimal management relies on timely surgical intervention coordinated by multidisciplinary care and appropriate resource availability, all of which may vary between hospital settings. Differences between trauma hospitals and non-trauma hospitals may influence outcomes, yet these variations have not been well characterized.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of hip fracture cases over a 2-year period (October 2022 to August 2024), comparing patient and procedural characteristics between a Level II trauma hospital (TH) (n = 104) and a non-trauma hospital (NTH) (n = 31). Polytrauma patients were excluded. Data were extracted from the electronic medical record (EMR). Primary outcomes were hospital length of stay (LOS) and time from admission to surgery. Group comparisons utilized chi-square or Fisher's exact tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U or Welch t-tests for continuous variables, as appropriate. A multivariable random forest model was used to evaluate predictors of operative duration.

RESULTS: ASA physical status distribution differed significantly between facilities (p = 0.03), with more ASA > 2 patients at the NTH (76.6% vs. 65.7%). Osteosynthesis was performed in 73.3% of NTH cases and 82.2% of TH cases; arthroplasty comprised 26.7% and 17.8%, respectively. LOS differed significantly by facility (p < 0.01), with a shorter mean stay at the NTH (4.3 vs. 5.9 days; mean difference, -1.73 days). Time to surgery also differed significantly (p < 0.001): mean 846 min (95% CI, 615-1078) at the NTH vs. 2686 minutes (95% CI, 2391-2981) at the TH. In multivariable modeling, procedure type was the dominant predictor of operative duration (permutation importance 0.686), followed by payer type (0.216); facility identity contributed minimally (0.034) after accounting for case mix.

CONCLUSION: Hip fracture care differed meaningfully between the TH and NTH within the same health care system. The NTH demonstrated significantly shorter time to surgery and LOS despite treating a proportionally higher-acuity patient population by ASA classification. These findings highlight opportunities for optimizing timeliness and resource allocation in hip fracture management across hospital settings and questions whether THs are the optimal location to treat these injuries.

BACKGROUND: Emergency care capacity remains critically limited in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly in rural areas where specialists and infrastructure are scarce. In Cambodia, stroke and ischemic heart disease are leading causes of mortality, and trauma burdens are increasing alongside rapid infrastructure development. Evidence on emergency equipment availability and frontline provider skills at the facility level in rural provinces remains limited.

METHODS: A facility-based cross-sectional assessment was conducted across all seven public referral hospitals in Battambang Province, Cambodia, in January 2023. Emergency equipment availability was evaluated through structured interviews and direct visual confirmation against the World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care. Clinical skill examinations were administered to physicians (two scenario-based cases: acute stroke with airway compromise; traumatic injury with tension pneumothorax and intra-abdominal bleeding) and nurses (a Basic Life Support [BLS] scenario assessed in pairs). Hospitals were stratified by Complementary Package of Activities (CPA) level: CPA1 (basic care only), CPA2 (including surgery and intensive care), and CPA3 (highest provincial level).

RESULTS: At Complementary Package of Activities (CPA)1 (basic care only) hospitals, intubation equipment and 12-lead electrocardiogram were each available in only 25% of facilities. None had a crash cart, blood transfusion capacity, basic metabolic panel, or coagulation testing. In the stroke scenario, airway patency was confirmed by 28.6% of physicians at CPA1 hospitals, compared with 70.0% at CPA2 hospitals (including surgery and intensive care), 57.1% at the CPA3 hospital (highest provincial level), and 75.0% at the Provincial Health Department. In the trauma scenario, no physician at CPA1 hospitals correctly performed spinal immobilization with the spine kept straight or thoracentesis at the correct anatomical location. Among 38 nurse pairs, 97.4% initiated chest compressions promptly, but only 21.1% demonstrated correct compression technique, and 13.2% provided effective bag-valve-mask ventilation. Deficiencies in equipment and clinical skills were most pronounced at CPA1 hospitals.

CONCLUSIONS: Emergency care capacity in Battambang Province was substantially limited, with the greatest deficiencies at CPA1 hospitals. Recurrent low-cost training and targeted strengthening of basic emergency care should be prioritized at lower-level facilities.

item.title: A scoping review evaluating artificial intelligence applications across various injury prevention domains.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [Systems/QI, TBI] [strong match]
Othman Y, Kasabwala D, Jayagopi K et al.

INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly utilized for injury prevention across diverse clinical and community settings including machine learning (ML). This scoping review aimed to synthesize the current literature on the applications and predictive performance of AI across multiple injury prevention domains.

METHODS: This scoping review searched five major databases, including PubMed, Embase, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, and the Cochrane Library, to identify studies evaluating AI applications for injury prevention published through May 2026. Eligible studies included original U.S.-based, English-language research across self-harm and suicide, abuse and violence, fall prevention, and sports injury prediction. Studies were excluded if they lacked measurable prevention outcomes or sufficient methodological detail, or focused on injury treatment rather than prevention, to ensure relevant and interpretable evidence for synthesis.

RESULTS: Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. ML models generally outperformed or matched traditional screening methods for self-harm and suicide prediction (AUC 0.81-0.82), while multimodal approaches achieved the highest predictive accuracy (AUC 0.90). In abuse and violence prevention, AI predicted intimate partner violence with an AUC of 0.88 and identified cases before formal disclosure. AI also improved fall risk assessment by accurately categorizing patient risk levels, predicting future falls, and mitigating fall injuries through wearable airbag technology. ML models predicted future sports-related injuries (AUC 0.76-0.84), while identifying modifiable risk factors including workload, strength deficits, prior injury burden, and concussion history.

CONCLUSION: ML-based prediction showed promise for risk stratification in self-harm, suicide, intimate partner violence, and recurrent victimization. Additionally, AI predicted fall risk and identified athletes at risk for future sports-related injuries while detecting modifiable risk factors, including workload, prior injury burden, and strength deficits. Although these findings suggest that AI and ML may have potential applications in supporting earlier risk identification, informing targeted prevention strategies, and facilitating more personalized approaches to injury prevention, the limited available evidence warrants careful interpretation.

BACKGROUND: Chronic wound healing remains a complex biological process influenced by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, microbial invasion, and insufficient tissue regeneration. Therefore, the design of multifunctional biomaterials that integrate structural support with biological regulation has emerged as a promising strategy in advanced wound care. This study sought to develop a composite hydrogel incorporating decellularized amniotic membrane (dAM)-derived extracellular matrix components alongside Matricaria chamomilla extract, with the goal of achieving enhanced regenerative and therapeutic outcomes.

METHODS: A CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel was prepared using decellularized dAM and subsequently evaluated in terms of its physicochemical and biological characteristics. The effectiveness of the decellularization process and preservation of ECM components were first examined, followed by characterization of hydrogel morphology, rheological properties, swelling and degradation behavior, and pH stability. Its biological performance was further assessed through hemocompatibility, cytocompatibility, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial assays, as well as a full-thickness wound model.

RESULTS: Incorporation of dAM and chamomile extract resulted in a stable hydrogel with favorable physicochemical and biological characteristics. The decellularization procedure removed 97.9% of the DNA. The resulting composite hydrogel exhibited an average pore size of 78.3 ± 9.8 µm, and all hydrogel formulations showed hemolysis rates below the 5% threshold accepted for blood-contacting biomaterials, with values ranging from 3.8% to 4.5%. The composite hydrogel also supported enhanced fibroblast viability (109.6 ± 11.3%) and demonstrated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial activities against wound-associated pathogens. In vivo, treatment with CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM accelerated wound closure (85.7 ± 6.3% at day 14) and supported tissue regeneration, outperforming both the dAM-containing hydrogel (78.9 ± 9.9%) and the commercial DuoDERM dressing (58.9 ± 4.5%), as evidenced by improved re-epithelialization, collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and early signs of tissue remodeling.

CONCLUSION: The CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel combines a dAM-containing extracellular matrix scaffold with chamomile-derived bioactive compounds, creating a favorable microenvironment for tissue repair. The addition of chamomile extract to the dAM-containing scaffold was associated with improved wound closure and tissue regeneration. While the present study design does not permit a definitive assessment of synergy between dAM and chamomile, these findings support the potential of this formulation as a multifunctional biomaterial platform for advanced wound healing applications.

BACKGROUND: Fracture nonunion remains a challenging clinical problem associated with prolonged disability and repeated surgical interventions. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been proposed as a biological adjunct to enhance bone healing; however, clinical evidence remains inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of PRP in the management of fracture nonunion.

METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO Registration: CRD420261366849). PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception to March 2026. Studies evaluating PRP in fracture nonunion and reporting union rate or time to union were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to compare PRP with control interventions. Risk ratios (RR) were calculated for union rates and standardized mean differences (SMD) for time to union. Additional single-arm analyses were performed to estimate pooled outcomes in PRP-treated cohorts.

RESULTS: Twenty-one studies comprising 877 patients were included. Two comparative studies (n = 119) demonstrated a higher likelihood of union with PRP (RR 1.17, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01-1.36, p < 0.05) without significant heterogeneity. Six studies (n = 250) showed no significant difference in time to union between PRP and control groups (SMD -0.72, 95% CI -1.48-0.05), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 85%). In PRP-only analyses, the pooled union rate was 0.86 (95% CI 0.76-0.94; I² = 61%) across seven studies (n = 150), and the pooled mean time to union was 6.08 months (95% CI 4.26-7.90; I² = 100%) across eight studies (n = 187).

CONCLUSION: PRP was associated with higher union rates in the limited comparative evidence, although no statistically significant difference in time to union was demonstrated. Heterogeneity in PRP protocols, methodological limitations, and the small comparative evidence base limit the certainty of these findings. PRP may have a potential role as a biological adjunct in fracture nonunion management, but further well-designed randomized controlled trials are required before definitive clinical recommendations can be made.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate baseline patterns of depression, behavioral health referral, and behavioral health treatment among orthopaedic trauma patients at a Level I trauma center.

METHODS: Design: Retrospective Cohort, Secondary Analysis Setting: Single Level 1 Trauma Center Patient selection criteria: Adult orthopaedic trauma patients who completed an ambulatory postoperative visit between September 2024 and November 2025. Secondary outcomes included referral patterns by injury mechanism and six-month orthopaedic complications or unplanned healthcare utilization.

RESULTS: Among 528 patients, 44.7% (236/528) screened positive for depressive symptoms, and 21.2% (112/528) demonstrated moderately severe to severe depression triggering a behavioral health referral. 33.9% (38/112) of referred patients completed a behavioral health visit compared with 67.6% (115/170) of referred non-trauma orthopaedic patients. The severe depression cohort was on average younger and more likely to be female, black, and have Medicare/Medicaid insurance status. Injury Severity Score did not differ significantly across depression categories. CONCLUSIONS: Significant gaps exist in the depression care cascade for orthopaedic trauma patients. Referral completion rates were approximately two-fold lower than non-trauma orthopaedic subspecialties, and referral non-completion was associated with significantly higher rates of infectious complications and unplanned healthcare utilization. Targeted, navigation-based interventions addressing structural barriers at the point of care are needed to close the gap between depression identification and treatment engagement in orthopaedic trauma.

Ayrton Senna, a three-time Formula 1 (F1) motorsport world champion from Brazil, met his tragic demise at the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix F1 race in Imola, Italy, after a devastating accident led to multiple skull base injuries and severe traumatic brain injury. The purpose of this study was to analyze the life and legacy of Senna, including his accident and injuries, forensic details surrounding his death, and the subsequent safety review and implementation of improved safety standards throughout F1 racing. Senna's accident, which was found to have resulted from steering column failure, helped shape the future of motorsport safety. Investigations into safety protocols and vehicle mechanisms revealed several shortcomings, resulting in multifaceted reform including introduction of the head and neck support device, changes in helmet design, track and barrier safety improvements, more stringent approval requirements for affiliated medical staff, new driver extrication measures, and a new seat belt standard. Senna's death further accelerated multidisciplinary safety reforms in motorsport medical care and prompted reassessments of acute on-track medical evaluations, specifically neurological evaluations. The combined contributions of Senna's close friends (including Dr. Eric Sidney "Sid" Watkins), the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile, and the Instituto Ayrton Senna have aided in developing robust safety standards that have prevented such tragedies for decades.

BACKGROUND: Peritoneal surface malignancies (PSM) are primary or secondary neoplastic deposits involving the peritoneum and are commonly associated with colorectal, gastric, appendiceal, gynecological, pancreaticobiliary, and other intra-abdominal or extra-abdominal cancers. Malignant bowel obstruction (MBO) is one of the most frequent and clinically consequential emergency presentations in this population, yet diagnostic and therapeutic pathways remain heterogeneous. We aimed to develop evidence-informed recommendations for emergency management of MBO in patients with PSM by integrating a systematic review, meta-analysis and a structured international expert consensus process.

METHODS: This systematic review, meta-analysis, and Delphi consensus followed PRISMA, Cochrane, and relevant MOOSE reporting principles. PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to June 2025 (English language). Five predefined PICO/PIRT questions addressed: (1) the diagnostic role of CT, plain abdominal X-ray, or Gastrografin-enhanced X-ray in PSM-related MBO; (2) nonoperative medical management versus surgical or endoscopic therapy; (3) surgical versus endoscopic treatment after failure of nonoperative management; (4) bowel resection versus stoma or bypass in surgical candidates; and (5) endoscopic stenting versus endoscopic ultrasound-guided bypass with lumen-apposing metal stents in endoscopic candidates. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently and in duplicate. Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for comparative non-randomized studies and MINORS for non-comparative studies; certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE. Random-effects meta-analyses (REML) produced odds ratios (OR), mean differences (MD), pooled means, or pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CI); heterogeneity was summarized using I2, τ2, and 95% prediction intervals. Evidence profiles informed statements voted on by the WSES-PSOGI-SICO expert panel during the 2025 WSES Congress.

RESULTS: No comparative diagnostic study evaluated abdominal X-ray or Gastrografin-enhanced X-ray in PSM-related MBO; two small retrospective CT-based series supported contrast-enhanced CT for mapping obstruction and excluding urgent complications, but no diagnostic meta-analysis was possible. For medical versus procedural treatment, medical management was associated with lower morbidity (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07-0.39) and shorter length of stay (MD - 9.48 days, 95% CI - 12.65 to -6.32), while success, mortality, and overall survival remained inconclusive. For surgery versus endoscopy, surgery showed higher clinical success (OR 2.57, 95% CI 1.47-4.50), whereas endoscopy shortened hospital stay (MD 3.35 days, 95% CI 1.46-5.23); mortality did not differ (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.70-1.49). Among surgical options, resection showed a signal toward higher perioperative mortality than bypass or ostomy (OR 3.55, 95% CI 1.45-8.68). Endoscopic stenting showed a pooled clinical success rate of 0.71 (95% CI 0.62-0.79), whereas evidence on LAMS was limited to one retrospective study. All guideline statements reached 100% agreement among voting participants.

CONCLUSIONS: Despite the low certainty of available evidence, integration of systematic review findings with expert consensus provides a structured international framework to support decision-making in emergency presentations of PSM-related MBO. These consensus-based recommendations are intended to assist clinicians in harmonizing care across peripheral and referral hospitals, while emphasizing individualized multidisciplinary judgement and the need for future higher-quality evidence.

item.title: Rural Pathologies: A Late Presentation Special.
item.description:
Emerg Med Australas | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]
Botha NC

Patients in rural and remote Australia often present later and with more advanced disease compared to major and regional cities. Drawing on experience as a junior doctor in the Cape and in rural emergency departments, this article explores how geographic isolation, limited resources, health literacy challenges and inequities in access shape these presentations. Cases include a critically unwell patient managed overnight in a makeshift intensive care bay when weather delayed retrieval, a family of young children with Norwegian Scabies, and a partial finger amputation complicated by weekend staffing shortages. The article reviews Australian evidence on sepsis, scabies and its link to rheumatic heart disease and trauma outcomes, all of which tend to be more challenging to manage. Timely care in rural and remote communities depends on early recognition, clear communication and close collaboration between rural generalists, FACEMs, retrieval services and specialist teams.

item.title: Predictors of 30-day mortality and complications following surgical treatment of pathologic hip fractures.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Thomas G, Njoku-Austin CO, Almeida ND et al.

Pathologic hip fractures present complex challenges and are associated with higher postoperative complication rates and mortality compared with non-pathologic fractures. This study aimed to compare 30-day outcomes between pathologic and non-pathologic hip fracture patients and identify factors associated with 30-day mortality and postoperative complications among patients with pathologic hip fractures using the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database. A retrospective analysis was conducted from 2006 to 2023. Patients aged ≥ 18 years undergoing hip fracture surgery were included. Patients with non-pathologic hip fractures were compared with those with pathologic hip fractures. Univariate analyses and multivariable logistic regression models were used to identify factors associated with pathologic hip fracture 30-day mortality and complications. Among 204,675 hip fracture patients, 6159 (2.9%) had pathologic hip fractures. Patients with pathologic hip fractures had higher rates of 30-day mortality (7.8% vs. 5.1%, p < 0.001), any postoperative complication (35.3% vs. 30.2%, p < 0.001), cardiac/transfusion complications (27.5% vs. 22.2%, p < 0.001), renal complications (0.5% vs. 0.3%, p = 0.017), and venous thromboembolic complications (3.4% vs. 1.7%, p < 0.001). Infectious complications and neurological complications were not significantly different between groups. In multivariable analyses, prominent protective factors associated with decreased 30-day mortality included absence of disseminated cancer (aOR 0.4, p < 0.001), independent functional status (aOR 0.2, p < 0.001), and absence of sepsis history (aOR 0.4, p = 0.02). Thrombocytopenia (aOR 1.9, p < 0.001) and anemia (aOR 1.9, p < 0.001) were prominent risk factors for 30-day mortality. Thrombocytopenia and anemia were also significant risk factors for any complications and cardiac/transfusion complications. These findings underscore the importance of comprehensive preoperative assessment and multidisciplinary care to optimize outcomes for patients with pathologic hip fractures. Patients with multiple risk factors for adverse postoperative morbidity and mortality should receive appropriately tailored care.

item.title: Video-assisted resident education is associated with improved ankle joint reduction: A prospective controlled study.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Orthopaedic, Systems/QI] [weak match]
Bilodeau RE, Hall AJ, Como M et al.

BACKGROUND: Proper fracture reduction and splinting technique is critical for soft tissue protection and fracture stability in the acute management of ankle fractures. However, residency education for acute ankle fracture reduction and splinting techniques remains poorly standardized and streamlined. This study evaluated the effect of implementing a video-assisted ankle fracture management education program administered to first-year orthopaedic residents on ankle joint reduction and splint quality.

METHODS: This was a prospective controlled study conducted at a single level I trauma center. All consecutive ankle fractures (OTA/AO: 4F, 44) requiring the placement of a bivalved short leg cast or AO splint from January 1, 2019, to June 30th, 2022 were included. Exclusion criteria included skeletal immaturity, missing imaging, delayed fracture presentation more than two weeks from injury, concurrent ipsilateral injury/polytrauma interfering with ankle reduction, open fracture, or ankle fractures treated without an AO splint or cast. The primary outcome was joint reduction quality defined as radiographic post-reduction tibiofibular overlap, tibiofibular clear space, and medial clear space. Secondary outcomes included splint padding thickness and ankle dorsiflexion angle to assess splint quality.

RESULTS: A total of 280 consecutive ankle fracture cases were included for evaluation of splint quality: 111 in the intervention group (mean age 46; [range 14-92]; 44% female) versus 169 in the control group (mean age 44; [range 14-90]; 41% female). Comparable injury severity was observed between groups. In the supination-external rotation IV (SER4) and type IV-equivalent (SER4e) subgroup, there was significant improvement in joint reduction quality in the intervention group as compared to control (55% versus 36%, respectively; Risk Ratio: 1.52, [95% CI: 1.03-2.25], p = 0.04). In the entire cohort, splint padding thickness was not significantly improved in the intervention group (p > 0.05), however, there was a significant increase in the percentage of ankles splinted in an appropriately dorsiflexed position (p = 0.03).

CONCLUSIONS: Implementation of video-assisted ankle fracture management education program was associated with improvements in overall ankle joint reduction quality. While the clinical significance of the improvements observed in ankle reduction remains yet to be established, orthopaedic surgery residency programs should consider incorporating video technique guides into their educational curricula.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, Therapeutic Study.

item.title: Disparities in investigation of physical abuse among trauma patients.
item.description:
Am J Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Penetrating, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Tarantino B, Buck M, Alicea J et al.

BACKGROUND: Physical abuse is a significant public health issue in the United States, leading to poor health outcomes such as chronic illness, depression, and substance abuse. Research regarding how the medical system addresses physical abuse in the overall adult population is scarce. The objective of this study was to assess disparities in investigation of physical abuse among adult trauma patients.

METHODS: This is a retrospective analysis of the 2017-2019 American College of Surgeons-Trauma Quality Program database. This study included all adult patients (≥18 years) who had a report of physical abuse by the medical team to authorities. Chi square and multivariate analysis were applied where appropriate to assess which characteristics showed disparities in investigation rate.

RESULTS: On univariate analysis, there were disparities with regard to age, mechanism, race, ethnicity, payment method, and mental health or substance use disorder. On multivariate analysis, male sex, non-penetrating trauma, age ≥70, American Indian race, and presence of a mental health disorder were associated with decreased odds of investigation. Non-elderly adult patients made up a disproportionate amount of abuse victims.

CONCLUSIONS: This study shows significant disparities in the escalation of a physical abuse report to an official investigation in the trauma setting. The authors recommend increased advocacy and resource allocation for these vulnerable populations in the clinical setting as well as further research regarding to what extent patient choice versus discretion of authorities influences these disparities. The authors also recommend a larger research focus on non-elderly adult victims of abuse.

item.title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune-pulmonary vulnerability.
item.description:
Intensive Care Med | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, TBI] [strong match]
Martin-Loeches I, Povoa P, Robba C et al.

BACKGROUND: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is frequent after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its biological meaning and outcome impact remain incompletely defined. Traditional models emphasise mechanical ventilation, aspiration, colonisation, endotracheal tube biofilm, and hospital pathogens. These mechanisms remain essential, but they do not fully explain the early clustering, heterogeneous susceptibility, changing bacteriology, and variable mortality effect observed after TBI.

MAIN TEXT: Severe brain injury creates an early vulnerable host state through impaired consciousness and airway protection, neuroimmune dysregulation, autonomic and endocrine activation, altered pulmonary immune surveillance, and, in many patients, extracranial trauma, shock, transfusion, or thoracic injury. These processes interact with ventilation, antibiotic pressure, and rapid respiratory microbiome disruption. Early VAP may reflect abrupt loss of control after injury and intubation, whereas late VAP may reflect persistent or secondary failure driven by biofilm maturation, antibiotic selection, multidrug-resistant pathogens, and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired immune dysfunction. Clinically, VAP consistently prolongs ventilation, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and resource use, while its independent effect on mortality is phenotype- and context-dependent.

CONCLUSIONS: This model proposes a timing-sensitive ecological framework in which established mechanisms may converge early and with particular clinical intensity after severe TBI, creating a vulnerable host-microbe state that may lower the threshold for clinically apparent infection. Future studies should distinguish isolated TBI from polytrauma, compare TBI with other acute brain injuries and non-neurological ventilated populations, and incorporate dynamic immune, microbial, and trajectory-based outcomes.

HIGHLIGHTS: VAP after TBI should be viewed as a timing-sensitive interaction between ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not as a distinct disease entity or as a pneumonia pathway unique to traumatic brain injury. The TBI-focused contribution lies in the early convergence of otherwise non-unique mechanisms: impaired airway control, aspiration risk, neuroimmune-endocrine activation, treatment exposure, dysbiosis, and extracranial injury burden, rather than in any single TBI-specific mechanism. Isolated TBI and TBI with polytrauma are biologically different phenotypes and should be separated in future studies. Early and late VAP may represent different phases of loss of pulmonary host-microbe containment; this distinction is probabilistic rather than TBI-specific in itself and requires validation in TBI-stratified cohorts. Mortality remains clinically relevant but context-dependent; VAP more consistently modifies recovery trajectory, ventilator dependence, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and possibly neurological recovery.

item.title: 24-hour risk updating for major ICU complications after severe trauma: a prospective cohort study.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Sanchez C, Cachafeiro L, Millan P et al.

PURPOSE: Conventional trauma prognostic models rely primarily on admission data and cannot account for subsequent physiological response to treatment. We evaluated whether routinely collected physiological information available at 24 h provides incremental prognostic information for major intensive care unit (ICU) complications in severely injured patients.

METHODS: We conducted a prospective cohort of adults with severe trauma (Injury Severity Score [ISS] ≥ 15) admitted to the ICU between January 2024 and April 2025. The primary outcome was a composite of major respiratory, hemodynamic, renal, or septic complications during the ICU course. TRISS was compared with an admission ridge model incorporating ISS, Glasgow Coma Scale, hemoglobin, lactate, and international normalized ratio, and a 24-h updated ridge model additionally incorporating 24-h lactate and change in creatinine. Performance was internally validated with 1,000 bootstrap resamples.

RESULTS: Among 109 patients, median ISS was 29 (IQR 20-38), and 73 (67.0%) developed major ICU complications. Optimism-corrected AUCs were 0.788 for TRISS, 0.873 for the admission model, and 0.887 for the 24-h updated model; Brier scores were 0.178, 0.140, and 0.131. Compared with the admission model, the 24-h updated model improved performance (ΔAUC 0.016, 95% bootstrap interval 0.004-0.030; ΔBrier - 0.010, - 0.017 to - 0.005). Twenty-four-hour lactate and creatinine change were the strongest contributors to the update.

CONCLUSION: In severely injured ICU patients, incorporating physiological evolution during the first 24 h refined admission-based prognostic assessment. Lactate and creatinine trajectories provided incremental information for major ICU complications during the ICU course. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

item.title: Maternity versus non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy.
item.description:
Cochrane Database Syst Rev | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]
Cryns N, Schroer J, Noel-Storr AH et al.

RATIONALE: Substantial uncertainty exists regarding how healthcare system factors, especially care setting types, affect the uptake and implementation of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy screening in practice. Evidence suggests that the care environment may influence diagnostic processes.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of maternity and non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus or diabetes in pregnancy.

SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) up to April 2026, and for controlled non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs) up to December 2025. We also searched CENTRAL to identify ongoing trials.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included RCTs and planned to include cluster-RCTs and NRSIs, but we did not find any. Eligible participants were pregnant women being screened for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or diabetes in pregnancy. We defined maternity healthcare settings as those specialising in care for pregnant, birthing, and postpartum individuals, with appropriate screening protocols, and non-maternity healthcare settings as general medical environments lacking a focus on pregnancy and women's care. We considered any screening format (e.g. risk-factor-based screening) and any diagnostic test (e.g. one- and two-step oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT)).

OUTCOMES: Critical health service outcomes were compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines, diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy, maternal emergency department visits during pregnancy, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisation, length of neonatal hospitalisation, and care accessibility. Critical maternal outcomes included hypertensive disorders, maternal death, intensive care admissions, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance, including progression to diabetes, within 15 years after birth. Critical child-related outcomes encompassed perinatal death, neonatal intensive care admissions, preterm birth, neonatal hypoglycaemia, large-for-gestational-age, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. Further critical and important outcomes not included in the summary of findings tables can be found in the full text.

RISK OF BIAS: We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool to assess bias in the RCTs. We had planned to use ROBINS-I version 2 to assess bias in the NRSIs if we had identified any.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We used standard Cochrane methodology. We planned to synthesise results for each outcome using meta-analysis where possible (inverse-variance or Mantel-Haenszel approaches; fixed-effect model). We used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We included one RCT with 781 participants: 390 were randomised to screening in a maternity healthcare setting and 391 were randomised to screening in a non-maternity healthcare setting. Except for screening compliance, trialists evaluated all outcomes using a per-protocol analysis instead of by original randomised groups. This approach created substantial disparities in sample sizes between settings and largely nullified the methodological protections typically provided by a randomised design. The trial evaluated screening for GDM only. We did not identify any ongoing studies or studies awaiting classification.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Health service outcomes Screening in a maternity healthcare setting may increase compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines (risk ratio (RR) 1.69, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.53 to 1.87; 781 participants) and may improve care accessibility, assessed as time to access antenatal diabetes care, measured in days (mean difference (MD) -4.70, 95% CI -6.03 to -3.37; 690 participants), both with low-certainty evidence. We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.01; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and length of neonatal hospitalisation (MD 0.04, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.65; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No direct evidence was available on screening for diabetes in pregnancy as distinct from GDM. No data were reported on maternal emergency department visits, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisations, and costs. Maternal outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on pre-eclampsia (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.75; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The following outcomes were not reported: eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, maternal death, admission to intensive care, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance. Child-related outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on: stillbirth or foetal death (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), admission to neonatal intensive care (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.71), preterm birth (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.41 to 2.71), neonatal hypoglycaemia (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.59), large-for-gestational-age (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.04), shoulder dystocia (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.70), and birth trauma (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), all with 690 participants each and very low-certainty evidence. An effect estimate for neonatal death was not estimable (maternity setting: 0/475; non-maternity setting: 0/215).

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: There is insufficient evidence to determine whether screening for gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy in maternity healthcare settings compared with non-maternity healthcare settings improves health service, maternal, or child-related outcomes. Low-certainty evidence from a single study indicates that screening in maternity healthcare settings may result in a reduction in time to access antenatal diabetes care and may increase compliance. The effects on other outcomes remain unknown. Conducting studies using intention-to-treat analyses could bridge existing research gaps, enhancing effect estimates and certainty.

FUNDING: This Cochrane review was funded by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the UNDP-UNFPA-UNICEF-WHO-World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP).

REGISTRATION: Protocol available via PROSPERO: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251108692.

item.title: Predictors of Return to Work Following Major Trauma in New Zealand.
item.description:
Emerg Med Australas | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Finlayson D, Logan S, Jemberie D et al.

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to identify physical and psychological predictors of return to work (RTW) in a cohort of major trauma patients in New Zealand.

METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at Christchurch Hospital involving patients identified from the New Zealand Major Trauma Registry. Full-time workers (n = 130) who sustained major trauma between 2016 and 2020 completed self-reported questionnaires assessing post-injury work capacity, PTSD (PCL-5), anxiety and depression (HADS) and perceived social support (MSPSS). Univariable and multivariable analyses were performed to determine predictors of decreased RTW following injury.

RESULTS: Older age, longer hospital length of stay (LOS) and ICU admission were all significantly associated with decreased RTW in the univariable analysis. Probable anxiety and depression were also significantly associated with decreased RTW, while meeting PTSD thresholds did not yield a significant association. In the final multivariable analysis, older age (OR 1.08, p < 0.01), longer LOS (OR 1.04, p = 0.048) and those with probable depression (OR 5.29, p = 0.01) were significantly associated with decreased RTW.

CONCLUSIONS: Probable depression is a strong, independent psychological predictor of reduced RTW following major trauma. These findings highlight the need for integrated post-trauma care models that incorporate routine psychological screening and early intervention to address both the physical and psychological needs of patients suffering from major trauma.

item.title: Variation in Pediatric Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Survival After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Development and Validation of a Survival Model for Risk-Standardized Survival Rates: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry.
item.description:
Crit Care Med | Tier 2 Filtered [Cardiac Arrest] [weak match]
Loaec M, Himebauch AS, Balcarcel D et al.

OBJECTIVES: To develop and internally validate a multivariable prediction model for survival to hospital discharge after pediatric extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA), and to use this model to derive risk-standardized survival rates (RSSRs) and quantify between-hospital variation in outcomes.

DESIGN: Retrospective multicenter cohort study.

SETTING: Hospitals contributing to the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry between 2020 and 2023.

PATIENTS: Children (< 18 yr) treated with ECPR for IHCA.

INTERVENTIONS: None.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Eligible patients were identified from the ELSO Registry and split into derivation (N = 1060) and validation (N = 317) cohorts using a hospital-stratified split to preserve within-hospital clustering. Survival prediction models were derived using penalized logistic regression with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. A full-event model incorporating 14 routinely available clinical variables demonstrated fair discrimination (area under the curve, 0.728 in the derivation cohort and 0.678 in the validation cohort) and good calibration (observed-to-expected ratio, 0.995; Brier score, 0.222 in the validation cohort). This model was embedded in a multilevel logistic regression model to generate hospital-level RSSRs for centers reporting five or more ECPR cases. Between-hospital variation was quantified using the median odds ratio, which was 1.30 (95% CI, 1.11-1.93), indicating significant differences in survival likelihood between centers after adjusting for patient-level risk.

CONCLUSIONS: In a large, international cohort of pediatric ECPR patients, we developed and internally validated a clinically interpretable model for survival to hospital discharge. The model performance as a discriminator likely limits its use as a standalone tool for clinical decision-making. However, strong internal calibration allowed for determination of hospital-level RSSRs, which revealed significant inter-hospital variability. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of developing a risk-adjustment model capable of estimating hospital-level RSSRs. Additional external validation and evaluation of residual case-mix differences are needed before such models can be used for benchmarking across pediatric ECPR centers.

item.title: Ischemic severity rather than ischemic time is associated with major limb complications in traumatic popliteal artery injury: A retrospective case series.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Izawa Y, Futamura K, Nishida M

PURPOSE: Although prolonged ischemic time is considered a key determinant of limb loss in traumatic popliteal artery injury (PAI), it does not fully explain the variability in clinical outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate whether ischemic severity at presentation is associated with major limb complications in PAI.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients with blunt PAI treated at a single trauma center between 2013 and 2025. Ischemic severity was assessed using the Rutherford classification and the presence of collateral circulation on computed tomography angiography (CTA). Patients were categorized into mild ischemia (Rutherford grade I-II) and severe ischemia (Rutherford grade III). Outcomes included extensive soft tissue defects requiring reconstruction and amputation.

RESULTS: Twenty-one limbs were included. Thirteen limbs were classified as mild ischemia and eight as severe ischemia. Collateral circulation was preserved in 17 limbs and absent in 4 limbs. The time to arterial reconstruction was comparable between groups. No major soft tissue complications occurred in the mild ischemia group. In contrast, 5 of 8 limbs with Rutherford grade III developed extensive soft tissue defects (p = 0.006). Absence of collateral circulation was also strongly associated with adverse outcomes, with all limbs without collateral flow developing major soft tissue complications (p = 0.002), despite a shorter time to revascularization.

CONCLUSION: Ischemic severity at presentation, particularly Rutherford grade III and absence of collateral circulation on CTA, is associated with major limb complications in traumatic PAI, whereas ischemic time alone may be insufficient to predict outcomes.

item.title: Traumatic Emergency Thoracotomy for Resuscitation in Shock (TETRiS): a national service evaluation of resuscitative thoracotomy practice outside the operating theatre.
item.description:
Resuscitation | Tier 2 Filtered [Cardiac Arrest, General Trauma, Penetrating, Prehospital, Systems/QI, Thoracic] [strong match]
Ramage L, Tucker H, Marsden ME et al.

BACKGROUND: Resuscitative thoracotomy (RT) is performed in patients with traumatic cardiac arrest or peri-arrest to treat potentially reversible causes of circulatory collapse. Optimal patient selection and timing remain uncertain, and existing evidence is largely retrospective, often excluding prehospital deaths. This prospective service evaluation examined contemporary RT practice and outcomes across a national major trauma system, including prehospital and emergency department settings.

METHODS: Prospective 12-month observational study across 20 UK Helicopter Emergency Medical Services and 26 Major Trauma Centre Emergency Departments, using the PHOTON, TERN, and NaTRIC research networks.

RESULTS: A total of 116 patients underwent RT, of which 82 (70.7%) were performed prehospital. Median age was 30 years, 97 patients (83.6%) were male, and 81 (69.8%) sustained penetrating injury. Suspected cardiac tamponade was the most common indication for RT (72/116 [62.1%]), although operative findings demonstrated exsanguinating haemorrhage in 82 patients (70.7%). Overall, 50 patients (43.1%) achieved return of spontaneous circulation and eight (6.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Survival was strongly associated with pathophysiological cause, duration of arrest, and physiological state at the time of intervention, with substantially better outcomes observed in patients with cardiac tamponade than exsanguination. Patients undergoing emergency department RT demonstrated shorter arrest durations, more favourable physiology, and higher survival than those undergoing prehospital RT. There were no survivors beyond 10 minutes of traumatic cardiac arrest.

CONCLUSION: In this prospective national evaluation of RT practice, outcomes were strongly associated with the pathophysiological cause and duration of arrest, and the residual physiology present at the time of intervention. The most favourable outcomes were observed in patients with cardiac tamponade and those undergoing RT before irreversible physiological deterioration.

item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]

BACKGROUND: CT-derived Hounsfield unit (HU) measurements may provide an opportunistic assessment of bone density when dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is difficult to obtain during acute treatment of femoral trochanteric fractures. We compared three femoral-head regions of interest (ROIs) and explored their ability to identify markedly low total hip bone mineral density (BMD).

METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included 87 women aged ≥ 65 years with AO/OTA type 31A1 (excluding A1.1) or 31A2 femoral trochanteric fractures treated with intramedullary nailing. Admission CT HU values were measured in three femoral-head ROIs on coronal and axial images and compared with contralateral hip DXA T-scores measured approximately 1 week after surgery. Pearson correlations and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed. The prespecified total hip T-score thresholds were ≤ -2.5 and ≤ -3.3; the latter was used as an operational definition of markedly low BMD in this study.

RESULTS: Coronal whole-femoral-head HU values (ROI 1) showed a moderate correlation with total hip T-scores (r = 0.569). For the ≤ -2.5 threshold, 74 women met the criterion and only 13 did not; the ROI 1 coronal AUC was 0.841. For the ≤ -3.3 threshold, 51 women met the criterion and 36 did not. A coronal ROI 1 threshold of < 158.7 HU had an AUC of 0.765 (95% CI, 0.660-0.870), sensitivity of 84.3% (43/51), and specificity of 66.7% (24/36) for identifying a total hip T-score ≤ -3.3.

CONCLUSION: Whole-femoral-head HU values were moderately associated with DXA-derived T-scores in this cohort. Admission CT may help flag patients with markedly low BMD, but the threshold showed limited specificity and requires external validation. Its effect on surgical decisions or clinical outcomes was not assessed.

item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Thoracic] [strong match]
Indorewala Y, Prashar S, Nishida C et al.

BACKGROUND: Retained hemothorax following tube thoracostomy occurs in up to one-third of thoracic trauma patients, often necessitating additional interventions. Thoracic irrigation has emerged as a potential adjunct to improve pleural drainage. The objective of this concise review is to evaluate the role of thoracic irrigation in the management of traumatic hemothorax by highlighting current standards of care and variations in techniques.

METHODS: This review searched five search engines, screening studies published before September 26, 2025. Studies focusing on thoracic irrigation in the setting of trauma and hemothorax were included.

RESULTS: A total of six studies were included. Thoracic irrigation in the management of traumatic hemothorax showed significantly lower odds of secondary intervention (OR: 0.16, p < 0.001) and shorter hospital length of stay (7 days vs. 9, p = 0.04) in patients who received thoracic irrigation compared with standard chest tube drainage. item.title: Scapular fracture and risk of great vessel injury in geriatric blunt trauma: A TQIP analysis.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI, Thoracic, Vascular] [strong match]
Peisepar M, Rafieezadeh A, Prabhakaran K et al.

INTRODUCTION: Scapular fractures are markers of high-energy blunt thoracic trauma and may indicate severe intrathoracic injury. Despite the substantial mortality linked with great vessel injuries (GVI), data specifically examining scapular fracture and GVI in the geriatric population remain limited. We hypothesized that scapular fracture, particularly when accompanied by concomitant thoracic fractures, is independently associated with GVI in geriatrics with blunt trauma.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Improvement Program (ACS-TQIP) database (2017-2023). Patients aged ≥ 65 years with a blunt mechanism of injury and AIS severity 2-5 in the neck, thorax, or upper extremity were included. GVI was defined using specific AIS codes for major thoracic and cervical vessels. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated association between scapular fracture patterns and GVI, including isolated scapular fractures, those with concomitant sternal, rib or flail chest fractures. Models adjusted for age, sex, race, mechanism, ISS, shock index, and modified frailty index. Vessel-specific analyses were also performed. Primary outcome was GVI. Secondary outcomes were mortality and LOS.

RESULTS: A total of 677,134 patients were included. Median age was 76 [70-82] years; 54.1% were female. Scapular fractures were identified in 5.0% of patients and GVI in 0.7%. In multivariable regression, isolated scapular fracture was associated with lower odds of GVI (aOR 0.783, 95% CI 0.704-0.871, p < 0.001), while scapular fracture with sternal fracture was associated with significantly higher odds (aOR 1.423, 95% CI 1.122-1.806, p = 0.004). Among vessel-specific analyses, subclavian artery injury demonstrated the highest association with scapular fracture (aOR 1.527, 95% CI 1.113-2.094, p = 0.009). GVI was associated with markedly higher in-hospital mortality (25.1% vs. 4.2%; OR 7.726, 95% CI 7.234-8.251, p < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: In geriatric blunt trauma, isolated scapular fracture is not an independent predictor of GVI. After a fall, a scapular fracture without a sternal fracture does not by itself suggest a missed vascular injury. In contrast, combined scapular and sternal fractures represent a high-risk pattern that warrants a heightened index of suspicion and a low threshold for CT angiography, with particular attention to the subclavian vessels.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/Epidemiologic; Level III.

item.description:

BACKGROUND: The benefit of routine early fecal diversion in blunt open pelvic fractures remains uncertain. We examined its association with pelvic infection and short-term mortality.

METHODS: MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and CENTRAL were searched from inception through 12 August 2026, with citation searching. Comparative observational studies were synthesized using crude risk ratios (RRs), REML random-effects models, modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals, and Mantel-Haenszel sensitivity analyses without continuity correction. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed ROBINS-I risk of bias and GRADE certainty.

RESULTS: Eighteen observational comparative reports were retained. Potential cohort overlap prevented a valid unique overall participant total. Eight cohorts contributed to broad pelvic infection (171 participants; seven estimable): RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.35-1.70; I²=19.6%). The stricter outcome-definition analysis included five cohorts (88 participants; four estimable): RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.07-6.97). Excluding two author-reported infected hematomas through an existing replacement sensitivity gave RR 0.84 (95% CI 0.34-2.05). Eight mortality cohorts (236 participants) yielded RR 0.82 (95% CI 0.33-2.07; I²=19.0%). Post-2006 evidence remained inconclusive for infection (three cohorts; RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.009-58.85) and mortality (five cohorts; RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.27-5.26). Diversion was preferentially used in patients with more severe injuries. All reports had Serious or Critical risk of bias; certainty was very low.

CONCLUSIONS: Available evidence does not establish a reduction in pelvic infection or short-term mortality with routine early diversion. Confounding, inconsistent outcome ascertainment, and imprecision prevent causal conclusions or exclusion of benefit in selected high-risk injuries.

item.title: Orthopedic trauma in patients with opioid use disorder: Current concepts in perioperative management.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Orthopaedic] [strong match]
Stout JW, Keenan J, Rehman S

BACKGROUND: Opioid use disorder (OUD) is an important challenge in orthopedic trauma, where acute injury intersects with preexisting opioid exposure, tolerance, complex pain, and barriers to continuity of addiction treatment. OUD has been associated with higher rates of complications, readmission, and treatment disruption, yet OUD-specific perioperative management remains inconsistently incorporated into orthopedic trauma practice. This review synthesizes the epidemiology, outcomes, and perioperative management evidence for this population.

METHODS: A clinically oriented current concepts review synthesized peer-reviewed literature, prioritizing studies published from 2013 onward. PubMed and Embase were searched, supplemented by Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, and manual review of reference lists from relevant articles. Studies examining perioperative outcomes, multimodal analgesia, and management of medications for OUD (MOUD) relevant to orthopedic trauma were included; studies limited to pediatric, elderly, or prenatal populations were excluded.

RESULTS: Preinjury opioid exposure is common among orthopedic trauma patients, whereas formally diagnosed OUD is less prevalent, affecting approximately 1% of operative trauma patients and up to 2.3% of patients with open lower-extremity fractures. OUD and opioid-related disorders are associated with higher rates of infection, nonunion, revision, prolonged hospitalization, and readmission. Consensus guidance and observational evidence support continuation of evidence-based MOUD, individualized opioid supplementation, multimodal nonopioid analgesia, regional anesthesia when appropriate, and early coordination with addiction and acute pain services. Guideline-based approaches to postoperative opioid prescribing, tapering, and patient education are also summarized.

CONCLUSIONS: Orthopedic trauma patients with OUD require individualized, multidisciplinary perioperative care. The strongest available evidence supports preservation of OUD treatment, multimodal analgesia, early addiction and pain consultation, and coordinated discharge planning rather than either opioid avoidance or opioid-only treatment. The review concludes with the authors' recommendations for the operating surgeon, including in-hospital and outpatient tapering plans, management of requests for additional opioids, and patient education.

BACKGROUND: Guidelines recommend surgical evacuation for traumatic subdural hematoma (SDH) with >5 mm midline shift (MLS), but emergency department (ED) triage varies between the operating room (OR) and the intensive care unit (ICU). We investigated whether ED disposition to the OR versus ICU was associated with differences in outcomes and whether distinct patient phenotypes modified these associations.

METHODS: We retrospectively identified adult patients from the ACS TQIP dataset with traumatic SDH, MLS >5 mm, and ED disposition to either the ICU or OR. We defined patient phenotypes using latent class analysis (LCA) and investigated associations between ED disposition and outcomes (inpatient mortality, favorable discharge) using risk-adjusted hierarchical logistic regression. We tested for interaction between patient phenotype and ED disposition and repeated these analyses among patients undergoing an ICU stay ≥1 day and cranial surgery.

RESULTS: Among 9582 patients, 29% (N = 2794) were triaged to the OR. Two LCA-informed phenotypes emerged: class 1 (older-mild injury) and class 2 (younger-severe injury). There was an interaction between ED disposition and patient phenotype, such that younger-severe patients had lower mortality with OR triage (P < 0.001). In the subgroup of 4573 patients (48%) with ≥1 day of ICU stay who underwent cranial surgery, there was a significant interaction between OR triage and the older-mild phenotype indicating increased mortality (P = 0.003).

CONCLUSIONS: For traumatic SDH with MLS >5 mm, triage the OR was associated with improved outcomes only among younger, severely-injured patients, while older, mildly-injured patients may benefit from early ICU stabilization. item.title: Fatal Opioid-Like Toxidrome Associated With a 7-Hydroxymitragynine Kratom Product.

Ann Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]

Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) use has increased in the United States, with the market shifting from traditional leaf preparations to concentrated products containing concentrated or chemically processed alkaloids such as 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-HMG) and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl. These formulations may deliver supraphysiologic opioid-receptor agonist doses with poorly characterized toxicity. A 42-year-old man was found dead at home after reportedly ingesting 3 tablets of a commercial "7-HMG" product and several beers. Postmortem examination revealed purge fluid at the mouth and nose, severe bilateral pulmonary edema, distended bladder, and no evidence of trauma or injection drug use. Quantitative analysis of the remaining tablet showed 29 mg 7-HMG and 0.58 mg mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, with minimal mitragynine. Postmortem blood contained 37.3 ng/mL 7-HMG and 76 ng/mL mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, whereas gabapentin and other medications were present at subtherapeutic concentrations. Compared with an estimated 1 to 4.5 mg 7-HMG in a typical high dose of dried kratom leaf powder, this ingestion delivered approximately 87 mg 7-HMG (19-fold to 87-fold greater 7-HMG exposure than a high-dose botanical leaf preparation). Given the high μ-opioid receptor activity of 7-HMG and its in vivo conversion to the even more potent opioid agonist mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, the postmortem findings are most consistent with a fatal opioid-like toxidrome associated with exposure to concentrated kratom alkaloids. This case illustrates the emerging risk posed by new kratom-branded products containing purified or chemically enriched alkaloids at doses far exceeding traditional preparations.

Pandey S, Chen Y, Yue JK et al.

STUDY OBJECTIVE: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is a prevalent and resource-intensive injury in the emergency department (ED). The blood-based biomarkers glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ubiquitin c-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) have demonstrated diagnostic potential for acute structural brain injury. Our objective was to clinically validate a US Food and Drug Administration-approved plasma test to aid in the identification of intracranial injury in patients with mTBI presenting to the ED and assess its integration with existing protocols.

METHODS: This single-center validation study enrolled 104 adult patients with suspected mTBI undergoing head computed tomography (CT) for evaluation between October 2023 and June 2024 at a Level I trauma center. Peripheral blood draw was completed within 12 hours postinjury and processed at the hospital clinical laboratory. Sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values for the test were calculated and compared with a standard clinical decision rule (Canadian Head CT Rule). ED length of stay and diagnostic turnaround times were examined.

RESULTS: Within the cohort (n=104), 83 patients had elevated biomarker levels (GFAP >30 pg/mL or UCH-L1 >360 pg/mL), and 11 patients had intracranial injury identified on CT. The combination plasma test demonstrated high sensitivity (0.91 [95% confidence interval {CI} 0.59 to 1.00]) but low specificity (0.22 [95% CI 0.14 to 0.31]) for predicting intracranial injury on CT with low positive predictive value (0.12 [95% CI 0.06 to 0.21]) and high negative predictive value (0.95 [95% CI 0.76 to 1.00]). These findings are consistent with prior studies (pooled sensitivity 0.97 [95% CI 0.95 to 0.98]; specificity 0.28 [95% CI 0.23 to 0.34]). False-positive cases (78%) were older than true-negative cases (median 72 years [interquartile range (IQR) 54 to 83] versus 58.5 years [IQR 38.25 to 66]). Median turnaround time for the GFAP/UCH-L1 test was 2 hours faster than head CT (1.09 hours [IQR 0.87 to 1.65] versus 3.28 hours [IQR 2.37 to 4.70]).

CONCLUSIONS: Blood biomarkers for mTBI have potential as an initial rule-out tool for intracranial injury prior to obtaining CT imaging; however, large multicenter studies are needed to clarify its impact on ED resource utilization, length of stay, and acute and long-term costs and benefits to patients and health care systems.

item.title: Prehospital Analgesia in Trauma: A Systematic Review of Current Evidence.
item.description:
Emerg Med Australas | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Prehospital] [strong match]
Alkoby-Meshulam L, Shahar C, Jacob R et al.

OBJECTIVES: Pain management is integral to prehospital trauma care. However, due to multiple challenges, pain is frequently undertreated despite important physiologic and psychologic implications. Among these challenges is uncertainty regarding the safety and effectiveness of pharmacologic agents administered enroute. We aimed to evaluate the level of evidence for the safety and effectiveness of prehospital pharmacologic analgesia for acutely injured adult trauma patients.

METHODS: An electronic database search of PUBMED, Google Scholar, Cochrane Library, Embase and Scopus for studies that reported on safety and/or effectiveness of prehospital pharmacologic analgesia for acutely injured adults (aged > 15 years) from January 1st, 2014, to January 1st, 2026. Non-original studies, paediatric studies, studies of non-pharmacologic agents or non-systemic administration (e.g., topical) were excluded.

RESULTS: Seventeen studies, involving 17,115 patients, met the inclusion criteria. The studies consisted of 6 randomized controlled trials, 5 retrospective cohort studies, one retrospective comparative study, one retrospective observational study, two prospective observational studies, one prospective cohort study and one non-randomized clinical trial. Agents included opioids, ketamine, methoxyflurane and paracetamol. Apart from one study of opioid therapy, no drug-attributed serious adverse events were reported. Minor adverse effects such as nausea, dizziness, dysphoria, agitation and drowsiness were common. All agents demonstrated effectiveness to varying levels.

CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence demonstrates an overall favourable safety and effectiveness profile of prehospital analgesia for adult trauma patients. However, considering the wide prehospital prevalence of injury-related pain, evidence is limited by scope, methodology and variations of treatment protocols.

INTRODUCTION: Modern asymmetric warfare and large-scale terror attacks produce distinctive wounding patterns that differ from conventional state-on-state conflict and impose specific early demands on receiving trauma systems. Variables were summarised as medians (IQR) or counts (percentages); missing data were not imputed and percentages were computed over non-missing observations.

BACKGROUND: Existing data suggests that hypocalcemia may be a factor in the lethal diamond of trauma. This could offer a potential opportunity for prehospital interventions to address these derangements. METHODS: We conducted a prospective multicenter observational study of trauma patients admitted at the highest level of activation for three participating centers where an ionized calcium level was measured upon arrival. Data from the prehospital records were collected from the Emergency Medical Services reports. We compared study variables between patients who were hypocalcemic, eucalcemic, and hypercalcemic.

RESULTS: There were 1270 participants enrolled in our primary study, of whom 1047 arrived by EMS from the scene meeting inclusion for this analysis. Of these, 235 were hypocalcemic and 39 were hypercalcemic upon arrival. Patients with calcium derangements had lower survival compared to patients without derangements. Of those who were hypocalcemic, 32.8% received prehospital blood products, compared to 25.6% of those who were hypercalcemic upon arrival. There were 5 (12.8%) who were hypercalcemic that received prehospital calcium, potentially indicating iatrogenic hypercalcemia. Elevated prehospital shock indices were associated with both derangements. Of the 718 who received no fluids or blood, 116 (16.1%) were hypocalcemic and 27 (3.7%) were hypocalcemic with 2 hypercalcemic participants receiving calcium. Of those 136 that received a blood product prehospital, 77 were hypocalcemic (56.6%) with 1 receiving calcium, and 10 (7.4%) were hypercalcemic with 3 receiving calcium, and the remaining were eucalcemic with 4 (2.9%) receiving calcium.

CONCLUSIONS: Both hypocalcemia and hypercalcemia occurred in the setting of blood product and no blood product administration. Our study suggests that currently available assessment methods are inadequate for predicting the presence of a calcium derangement, both high and low.

BACKGROUND: Severe trauma induces a cytokine storm that is associated with impaired resuscitation and recovery. METHODS: Hemorrhagic shock with polytrauma was induced in 64 Sprague-Dawley rats. The rats were randomized to receive one of four intravenous treatments at 15 minutes posthemorrhage (T15): saline control, AQB-565, tranexamic acid (TXA), or combined AQB-565+ TXA. Survival, hemodynamics, cytokine profiles, and hemorrhage volumes were compared between groups.

RESULTS: There was a significant overall effect of treatment group on MAP (two-way rmANOVA p=0.02) that coincided with blood transfusion. MAP was significantly increased at T105 with AQB-565+TXA versus saline control (p=0.046). PURPOSE: To investigate whether the addition of a McLaughlin cerclage to locking plate fixation of distal patellar pole fractures provides improved biomechanical construct stability and reduced interfragmentary displacement.

Subsequently, locking plate fixation was performed. In a randomized half of the specimens, an additional McLaughlin wire cerclage was applied. The specimens were then subjected to 3000 cycles of extension starting at 90° of flexion under a maximum tensile load of 320 N. Using a Digital Image Correlation (DIC) system, the interfragmentary displacement between the proximal and distal fragments was measured at 1, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 2000, and 3000 cycles. RESULTS: An additional McLaughlin cerclage significantly reduced interfragmentary displacement under cyclic loading in comparison to locking plate fixation alone. CONCLUSION: An additional McLaughlin cerclage reduced interfragmentary displacement in distal patellar pole fractures. In cases of unstable distal pole patella fractures, the additional use of a McLaughlin cerclage may therefore be considered to enhance construct stability.
