BACKGROUND: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) often requires repeat head computed tomography (CT) imaging to monitor for bleed progression. While prior literature has explored patient-level factors, data on the impact of ICH morphologies (subdural [SDH], epidural [EDH], intraparenchymal [IPH], intraventricular [IVH], and multicompartment hemorrhage [MCH]) on radiographic ICH progression remains unclear. We hypothesized that MCH and IVH would have an increased associated risk of progression.

METHODS: This retrospective (2021-2023) single-center cohort included adults (≥18 y) with TBI-related ICH who underwent initial and repeat head CT. Patients were stratified into radiographic progression versus no-progression cohorts, with progression defined as new or enlarging hemorrhage on attending radiologist interpretation of follow-up head CT. The primary outcome was the rate of radiographic progression for each ICH type. MCH was defined as the presence of two or more ICH types. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to evaluate the association between each ICH type and radiographic progression, adjusting for age, mechanism of injury, Injury Severity Score, Glasgow Coma Scale on arrival, trauma-bay intubation, and preinjury antithrombotic exposure.

RESULTS: Of the 817 patients with ICH on initial head CT and documented repeat CT, 401 (49.1%) had radiographic progression. Patients with progression were younger (58 vs. 62 y, p=0.027), more frequently male (71.3% vs. 63.7%, p=0.020), and had similar antithrombotic exposure (15.2% vs. 14.2%, p=0.678). Craniotomy/craniectomy was more frequent among those with progression (21.2% vs. 8.2%, p<0.001). On multivariable analysis, MCH demonstrated the strongest associated risk for progression (odds ratio [OR] 5.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.36-9.33, p<0.001), whereas IPH (OR 2.02, CI: 0.86-4.75, p=0.108), SDH, EDH, and IVH were not independently associated with radiographic ICH progression.

CONCLUSIONS: MCH was independently associated with radiographic ICH progression. This higher-risk hemorrhage pattern may warrant closer neurological monitoring.

item.title: A clinically relevant porcine model of flail chest: Development and multimodal validation.
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [Thoracic] [strong match]
Li S, Zhao Y, Liang Q et al.

BACKGROUND: Flail chest has high mortality, but large-animal models with thoracic anatomy comparable to humans are lacking. The objective of this study was to develop a clinically relevant porcine flail chest model that preserves pleural, pulmonary, and neurovascular integrity, and to validate it using multimodal assessment including computed tomography (CT) imaging and physiologic parameters.

METHODS: Twelve male Landrace pigs were randomly assigned to a flail chest (FC) group and a multiple single rib fracture (MRF) group (n=6 per group). Under general anesthesia, controlled osteotomies were performed on the fifth to eighth ribs. The intercostal neurovascular bundle was protected, and the parietal pleura was bluntly separated before each osteotomy to preserve pleural integrity. In the FC group, each rib was transected at two sites to create a four-rib flail segment; in the MRF group, a single transection was made per rib. Paradoxical chest wall motion was visually confirmed in the FC group before layered closure. Invasive arterial pressure, heart rate, pulse oxygen saturation (SpO₂), and end‑tidal carbon dioxide tension (ETCO₂) were monitored throughout. Chest CT was performed on Day 7.

RESULTS: All surgeries were successful, with no mortality. Paradoxical chest wall motion was confirmed in all FC animals after emergence. The SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio declined postoperatively in both groups, with a significantly greater decrease in the FC group than in the MRF group (221.0±1.4 vs. 260.2±1.9, P<0.001). Heart rate and mean arterial pressure increased in both groups and were significantly higher in the FC group (P<0.001). CT confirmed the intended fracture patterns and flail-segment displacement, with no evidence of pleural breach, pulmonary injury, pneumothorax, or hemothorax.

CONCLUSIONS: A standardized porcine flail chest model was established that preserves pleural, pulmonary, and neurovascular integrity, allowing the isolated study of rib fracture pathophysiology. This model will facilitate future research on fixation materials and surgical techniques.

item.title: Contemporary management of traumatic abdominal wall hernias: What you need to know.
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma] [strong match]
Dilday JC, Nikolian V, Martin MJ

Traumatic abdominal wall hernia (TAWH) is an uncommon but clinically important consequence of both blunt and penetrating abdominal trauma. It is defined by disruption of the abdominal wall musculature and fascia with herniation of intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal contents through the defect. Although penetrating abdominal wall defects are usually apparent and can often be primarily closed during operative exploration, blunt TAWH is significantly more heterogeneous and challenging. The skin may remain intact while the muscle, fascia, neurovascular supply, and bony attachments are disrupted. The reported incidence of TAWH varies according to imaging strategy and trauma population, but frank herniation remains rare, occurring in <1% of blunt trauma patients in most contemporary series. The major management challenge is deciding whether the patient requires immediate trauma laparotomy or laparoscopy, acute abdominal wall repair, staged management with same-admission repair, or delayed hernia repair/abdominal wall reconstruction. Evidence remains primarily dominated by retrospective single-center series, multicenter registry studies, and systematic reviews with heterogeneous definitions and follow-up. Although traditional dogma had taught that these repairs should always be performed in a delayed fashion, recent multicenter data, systematic reviews, and surgeon experience suggest that timing of repair, type of repair, and mesh use must be individualized; bowel injury, contamination, defect location, and patient physiology are more important than a universal early-versus-delayed algorithm. This article summarizes the practical issues the trauma and acute care surgeon needs to know: diagnosis, classification, associated injuries, indications for exploration, repair timing, operative strategy, management of lateral and posterior defects, mesh use in contaminated fields, and associated outcomes.

PURPOSE: Traumatic pelvic hemorrhage is a major driver of morbidity and mortality in pelvic fractures. Classic literature described pelvic hemorrhage as predominantly venous, whereas arterial injury is considered less common. We evaluated the frequency, anatomical distribution, and presumed sources of pelvic hemorrhage in a contemporary trauma cohort using contrast-enhanced CT (CECT).

METHODS: We conducted a single-center, retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients with pelvic fractures treated at a level-I trauma center between 2020 and 2022. All patients underwent CECT at initial presentation. Two experienced pelvic trauma surgeons independently reviewed all scans. Radiologically relevant hemorrhage was defined by contrast extravasation, soft-tissue asymmetry/displacement, or a contained intrapelvic hematoma. Patients with and without hemorrhage were compared regarding age, sex, trauma mechanism, anticoagulation, and fracture type. The presumed bleeding sources were categorized as arterial, venous, cancellous, or mixed.

RESULTS: Radiologically relevant hemorrhage occurred in 95/512 (18.6%) patients and was more frequent after high-energy trauma and in men. Iliac sites predominated, whereas presacral bleeding was uncommon. The presumed bleeding source was cancellous in 44.2%, mixed in 29.5%, arterial in 18.9%, and isolated venous in 7.4%. Overall mortality was 7.0% and was significantly higher in patients with hemorrhage (14.7% vs. 5.3%; p < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: In this contemporary CECT-based cohort, pelvic hemorrhage was less frequent than historically reported, with CT findings most commonly suggesting cancellous or mixed bleeding sources. AIMS: Trochanteric fractures (TF) are among the most frequent fractures and have major impact on the affected patients and the healthcare system. The TFN-A group had significantly more major revisions (hazard ratio 3.57 (95% confidence interval 1.42-9.94; p = 0.004). DISCUSSION: The TFN-A had a significantly higher rate of complications leading to major revision than the former PFN-A. This may have been missed when considering only the reoperation rate for all causes due to a camouflage effect by minor complications.

item.title: Acute hemorrhagic shock from vaginal laceration during intercourse requiring operative management.
item.description:
Am J Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [Haemorrhage] [strong match]
Nordt SP, Pham B

Vaginal laceration during consensual intercourse is a rare cause of acute vaginal bleeding. Most coital injuries are minor, although may result in acute hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability. A 30-year-old G3P2012 otherwise healthy woman presented to the emergency department (ED) with acute vaginal bleeding immediately during consensual intercourse. She was initially well-appearing then developed hemorrhagic shock in the ED from ongoing vaginal exsanguination. The bleeding source could not be visualized on speculum examination. She was resuscitated with tranexamic acid, crystalloid, and two units of unmatched whole blood and taken emergently to the operating room. Examination under anesthesia after evacuation identified a horizontal posterior vaginal wall laceration. The laceration was repaired transvaginally with hemostasis, and the patient recovered uneventfully. A vaginal laceration during intercourse may cause acute life-threatening hemorrhage. Bleeding is often occult on speculum examinations although may progress rapidly to shock. Emergency clinicians should exclude pregnancy, initiate early resuscitation, and urgently consult gynecology for examination under anesthesia and repair when indicated.

JAMA Surg | Tier 2 Filtered [Haemorrhage] [weak match]

IMPORTANCE: Female patients undergoing cardiac surgery have a higher transfusion burden, yet they remain underrepresented in randomized clinical trials. Although the ANH trial showed no significant reduction in the proportion of patients receiving allogeneic blood transfusions with acute normovolemic hemodilution, evidence regarding its efficacy and safety specifically in female patients remains limited.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of acute normovolemic hemodilution (ANH) compared with usual care in female patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This was a post hoc secondary analysis of the multicenter, randomized ANH trial, which was conducted at 32 centers in 11 countries from April 2019 to December 2024. Of 2010 patients in the original ANH trial, 405 were women and were included in this analysis; 219 had been randomized to receive ANH and 186 to usual care. This secondary analysis was conducted from August 2025 to January 2026.

INTERVENTION: Withdrawal of at least 650 mL whole blood with crystalloids replacement and reinfusion after cardiopulmonary bypass.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the occurrence of at least 1 allogeneic packed red blood cell (pRBC) transfusion during the index hospitalization. Safety outcomes included intraoperative hypotension, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, hospital length of stay, mortality, and other perioperative complications.

RESULTS: The median (IQR) age of the participants was 62 (54-69) years. The occurrence of allogeneic pRBC transfusion was similar in the ANH and usual care groups (38.8% vs 44.6%, respectively; relative risk [RR], 0.87; 95% CI, 0.69-1.10; P = .24). Intraoperative hypotension occurred more frequently with ANH (16.0% vs 4.8% in usual care; RR, 3.30; 95% CI, 1.62-6.74; P = .02). Patients receiving ANH also had longer ICU stays (mean difference, 21.13 hours; 95% CI, 1.89-40.38; P = .03) and hospital stays (mean difference, 1.92 days; 95% CI, 0.14-3.70; P = .04). No significant differences were observed in mortality or other postoperative complications.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this post hoc secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial, ANH was not associated with a reduction in allogeneic pRBC transfusion among women undergoing cardiac surgery and was associated with more frequent intraoperative hypotension and longer ICU and hospital stay. These exploratory findings warrant confirmation in adequately powered studies specifically designed to evaluate female patients undergoing cardiac surgery.

item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [weak match]
Süner U, Tunçez M, Sağıroğlu D et al.

PURPOSE: Although fifth metacarpal neck fractures are commonly managed conservatively, there is no consensus regarding the optimal immobilization strategy. The aim of this study was to compare the radiographic outcomes of the Jahss Position Splint (JPS) and the conventional Ulnar Gutter Splint (UGS) in the treatment of fifth metacarpal neck fractures.

METHODS: A total of 78 adult male patients treated for isolated closed fifth metacarpal neck fractures between January 2023 and June 2024 were prospectively evaluated. Patients were allocated to either the JPS group (n = 42) or the UGS group (n = 36). Patients were assigned to JPS or UGS according to the predefined odd/even-calendar-day duty schedule of two surgeons, each of whom routinely applied one of the techniques. All patients underwent closed reduction using the Jahss maneuver followed by three weeks of immobilization. Radiographic outcomes included initial fracture angulation (IFA), post-reduction angulation (PRA), final follow-up angulation at 12 weeks (FFA), metacarpal shortening, and malunion rates.

RESULTS: No significant differences were observed between the groups regarding age or IFA (p > 0.05). Correction during reduction and splint application was greater with JPS than with UGS (15.2 ± 9.6° vs. 8.9 ± 11.0°; p = 0.009), whereas subsequent loss of reduction during immobilisation did not differ significantly between the groups (2.8 ± 8.4° vs. 1.0 ± 9.8°; p = 0.388).The JPS group demonstrated significantly lower PRA (p < 0.001) and FFA (p = 0.003) compared with the UGS group. Metacarpal shortening was significantly less in the JPS group (p = 0.036). The malunion rate was 5% in the JPS group and 28% in the UGS group (p = 0.009).

CONCLUSION: JPS was associated with greater immediate angular correction and more favourable final radiographic outcomes than UGS but did not reduce subsequent loss of reduction during immobilisation. Because functional and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed, the clinical relevance of these radiographic differences remains uncertain.

item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [Facial/Neck, General Trauma] [weak match]
Boffano P, Lahtinen A, Brucoli M et al.

INTRODUCTION: Isolated orbital floor fractures in juveniles are a challenge, as children and adolescents may experience diplopia and limited ocular motility, even with little to no periorbital edema or visible signs of injury to the eye. The aim of the present study is to assess the demographic and clinical variables, and the outcomes of pediatric patients affected by isolated orbital wall fractures at several European oral and maxillofacial surgery centers.

METHODS: Pediatric patients (less than 18 years) with hospitalized and surgically treated for unilateral isolated orbital blow out fractures of the orbital floor and/or the medial wall were included. The following data were recorded for each patient: gender, age, etiology of trauma, site of orbital wall fracture(s), timing of intervention, surgical approach, orbital reconstruction material/implant, post-operative complications RESULTS: A total of 51 pediatric patients (45 boys, 6 girls) with a mean age of 12.1 years were included. Most patients (43 children, 84.3%) presented with an isolated orbital floor fracture. Clinically, the most frequently observed sign was diplopia / double vision (43 patients, 84.3%). More than two thirds (68.6%) of cases were surgically treated within the first two days from injury. In 6 patients (11.8%) one or more persistent postoperative disturbances were found six months postoperatively, including diplopia in 3 subjects (5.9%), infraorbital nerve paresthesia in 2 patients (3.9%), and enophthalmos in 2 patients (3.9%).

CONCLUSIONS: The rarity of pure orbital wall fractures in pediatric patients makes it difficult to establish uniform evidence-based guidelines for their management. These injuries must also be recognized promptly, as surgical intervention may be required at a very early stage. A reasoned and individualized choice of the optimal surgical approach appears to be the most appropriate strategy for this specific type of facial fracture in the pediatric population.

item.description:

PURPOSE: Moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures are associated with high morbidity and mortality despite advances in resuscitation, development in trauma systems and multispecialty haemorrhage control. This study aimed to describe the management strategies and clinical outcomes of moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures over a 10-year period at an Australian Level I Trauma Centre.

METHODS: A retrospective observational cohort study was performed of patients aged ≥ 16 years with moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures (Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) ≥ 3) treated between January 2015 and December 2024. Data were obtained from the institutional prospectively collected trauma registry.

RESULTS: A total of 313 patients met the inclusion criteria. The mean age was 47.0 years and 69.3% were male. Motor vehicle (35.1%) and motorcycle collisions (24.9%) accounted for 60.1% of injuries. Median ISS was 26 (IQR 19-34), with 70.6% sustaining pelvic AIS 4-5 injuries. 20.1% of patients underwent at least one haemorrhage-control intervention, including angioembolisation (14.4%), preperitoneal pelvic packing (5.8%) and external fixation (5.8%). Angioembolisation utilisation increased from 6.7% in 2015 to 40.0% in 2024. In-hospital mortality was 7.7%, with traumatic brain injury accounting for 62.5% of deaths and haemorrhagic shock for only one death.

CONCLUSION: Moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures remained characterised by high-energy mechanisms and severe multisystem injury over the study period, while management evolved with increasing utilisation of angioembolisation. In-hospital mortality was numerically lower compared with historical cohorts, with most deaths attributable to associated traumatic brain injury rather than pelvic haemorrhage.

item.title: Prehospital Care of Older Adults Following Perceived Low-Acuity Falls and Related "Lift Assist" Encounters: An NAEMSP Position Statement and Resource Document.
item.description:
Prehosp Emerg Care | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Prehospital] [strong match]
Dorsett M, Su TW, Farcas AM et al.

Older adults who present as low-acuity falls requiring mobilization assistance, commonly referred to as a "lift assist", represent a common reason for EMS activation. These encounters often involve underlying medical conditions or injuries that are not immediately apparent, and missed or delayed diagnosis is associated with adverse outcomes. At the same time, some patients are transported to the emergency department when it is not necessary, exposing them to potential harms and contributing to increased health care utilization. These encounters are therefore complex clinical presentations and represent important opportunities for thorough assessment and higher-order clinical decision making, supported by systems that enable appropriate disposition and follow-up. However, there is a system-level bias, beginning in initial education and reinforced through dispatch, policy, and protocol, that frames these encounters as uniformly low-acuity, non-medical, minor traumas leading to underassessment and limiting clinical decision-making. Therefore, NAEMSP recommends:EMS systems should recognize calls for falls or "lift assists" as patient encounters that warrant an assessment, including evaluation for underlying medical causes, traumatic injuries, and safety, and frame these encounters as opportunities for higher-order clinical decision-making within the broader context of geriatric syndromes rather than isolated low-acuity events.EMS systems should support transport decisions based on a thorough assessment and patient-centered discussion, recognizing that not all patients require ED transport and that safe alternatives may include non-transport or referral to appropriate follow-up pathways.EMS systems should track the assessment of patients encountered during "lift assist" responses and older adults following perceived low acuity falls as a system-level quality measure to monitor performance and drive improvement.Policymakers and payers should implement sustainable reimbursement structures that support EMS assessment and care even when transport does not occur.

BACKGROUND: Anterior shoulder dislocation is among the most common major joint dislocations presenting to the emergency department (ED) and is frequently managed with procedural sedation. Several analgesic and regional anesthesia strategies are available for shoulder reduction, each with distinct advantages and limitations. The Shoulder Anterior Capsular (SHAC) block is a superficial, ultrasound-guided interfascial plane technique that targets pericapsular nerve contributions to the glenohumeral joint via an anterior approach, offering a potentially motor-sparing and sedation-sparing alternative.

CASE PRESENTATION: We present two cases of ED anterior shoulder dislocation managed with the SHAC block at a high-volume Level 1 trauma center. In the first case, a 60-year-old male with recurrent dislocation underwent successful reduction without procedural sedation, reporting it as his least painful reduction among multiple prior experiences. In the second case, a 94-year-old female with a complex fracture-dislocation in cervical spine precautions received the SHAC block as an analgesic adjunct; although procedural sedation was ultimately required, the patient required no intravenous analgesia during a subsequent 36-h observation period. In both cases, the block was performed by an emergency medicine intern under supervision by a Pain Medicine fellowship-trained attending physician, preserving the ability to conduct post-reduction axillary nerve assessment.

CONCLUSION: The SHAC block was technically feasible in two selected patients with anterior shoulder dislocation and provided variable analgesia. Further study is needed to evaluate its efficacy, safety, positioning requirements, reproducibility, and appropriate patient selection.

item.description:
J Am Coll Surg | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Orthopaedic, Systems/QI, TBI] [strong match]
Ilkhani S, Figi JT, Thompson AA et al.

BACKGROUND: Recovery after traumatic injury may extend beyond conventional follow-up, but longer-term changes in function, quality of life (QoL), and return to work (RTW) remain incompletely characterized.

STUDY DESIGN: English- or Spanish-speaking patients with Injury Severity Score ≥9 from three US Level I trauma centers completed telephone surveys 6 and 12 months after injury. Recovery was characterized as improved, stable, or declined between timepoints. Function was assessed across six Trauma Quality of Life domains; QoL and RTW by self-report; and mental health using GAD-7, PHQ-8, and Breslau PTSD scales. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated predictors of QoL decline. Sensitivity analyses examined traumatic brain injury (TBI), isolated long bone fracture, and general trauma.

RESULTS: Among 1,894 patients, 49% of those impaired at 6 months improved, 41% were unchanged, and 11% worsened by 12 months. Patients ≥65 more often improved (20% vs. 16%) and declined (16% vs. 9%) than those <65; surgical patients more often improved (20% vs. 16%). QoL improved in 22%, remained stable in 56%, and declined in 22%. TBI patients had the greatest functional improvement (55%), whereas long bone fracture patients had the greatest QoL improvement (26%). Weak social support (aOR 3.68) and mental health symptoms were associated with QoL decline. RTW reached 61% by 6 months; 74% of non-returners remained so at 12 months.

CONCLUSIONS: Recovery remains dynamic beyond 6 months after trauma, supporting extended follow-up and individualized rehabilitation. Associations of mental health symptoms and weak social support with QoL decline support incorporating their assessment into post-injury care.

BACKGROUND: Evidence on surgical outcomes in active conflict settings remains limited, particularly regarding postoperative morbidity and its relationship to injury severity among civilians with severe war-related injuries. This study describes the pattern of postoperative morbidity following emergency surgery for conflict-related abdominal and thoracic trauma.

METHODS: We conducted a cohort study of patients undergoing emergency war trauma surgery at a single surgical unit during the 2024 Gaza conflict. Data were collected prospectively and supplemented through retrospective review when needed. To avoid conflating early postoperative death with an absence of morbidity, postoperative morbidity was described only among patients who survived to hospital discharge.

RESULTS: Seventy-nine patients were included. Five patients (6%) died intraoperatively and were excluded from postoperative analysis. Of the remaining 74 patients, 20 (27%) died during the index admission and 54 (73%) survived to discharge; non-survivors had substantially higher Injury Severity Scores than survivors (median ISS 32 vs 16) and were less often haemodynamically stable on arrival (12% vs 67%). Among the 54 survivors, postoperative morbidity occurred in 46 (85%), mainly due to infectious complications (81%), particularly surgical site infection (74%). Descriptive comparison of survivors with and without morbidity showed similar injury severity between groups (median ISS 16 vs 16.5), suggesting that once patients survived long enough to be at risk of complications, morbidity was common across the injury-severity spectrum rather than concentrated among the most severely injured.

CONCLUSIONS: Postoperative morbidity after conflict-related emergency surgery was high among survivors and was largely driven by infectious complications. Mortality, rather than morbidity, was most closely related to injury severity. These findings support the need for consistent injury severity assessment, improved infection prevention strategies, and cautious interpretation of morbidity data in conflict cohorts where early mortality limits the population at risk of developing recorded complications.

BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVE: Optimal ventilation delivery during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains uncertain. We evaluated the association between MV use during CPR and clinical outcomes in adults with cardiac arrest compared with manual BV.

METHODS: We searched 6 bibliographic databases from inception through May 31, 2026. Included studies compared MV and BV ventilation CPR in adult cardiac arrest patients. Patients receiving MV at any moment during CPR were classified as the MV group; those receiving only BV comprised the BV group. Primary outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital admission, survival to hospital discharge, and good neurological outcome. Secondary outcomes included physiologic variables and pneumothorax. We calculated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences with 95% credible intervals (CrIs) using Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses.

RESULTS: Eight studies involving 6847 patients were included. For the primary outcome, MV use during CPR was associated with a higher rate of ROSC than BV use (pooled RR, 1.20; 95% CrI, 1.04-1.42), with a 99% posterior probability of benefit. Posterior probabilities favoring MV for survival to admission, survival to discharge, and good neurological outcome were 92.3%, 93.6%, and 92.2%, respectively. Pneumothorax incidence was similar between groups.

CONCLUSION: In adult cardiac arrest, MV use during CPR was associated with higher ROSC compared with manual BV. Evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes remains imprecise and inconclusive.

BACKGROUND: Traumatic arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs), with or without associated pseudoaneurysms, are uncommon complications of penetrating vascular injuries that may cause substantial morbidity and potentially fatal complications. Evidence is largely derived from case reports and case series, with important contributions from military experience. Delayed gluteal lesions may mimic a hematoma or abscess, creating a diagnostic pitfall.

CASE PRESENTATION: A 51-year-old male presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging painful left buttock mass following a stab wound that had been primarily sutured at a local hospital. Initial ultrasound suggested a hematoma, and the patient was admitted with a working diagnosis of "left buttock mass." Physical examination revealed a 7 × 7 cm fluctuant mass with tenderness but without overt signs of infection. Contrast-enhanced pelvic CT demonstrated a 6.8 × 3.2 cm intensely enhancing lesion within the left gluteus maximus with prominent feeding vessels, suggestive of an arteriovenous fistula or vascular malformation. Digital subtraction angiography confirmed a left gluteal pseudoaneurysm with an associated arteriovenous fistula supplied by branches of both the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal arteries, with early venous opacification. The patient underwent successful transcatheter embolization using fibered platinum coils and a cyanoacrylate-lipiodol mixture, with complete occlusion of the fistula confirmed on completion angiography. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 2. At three-month follow-up, the patient reported no specific discomfort, and color Doppler ultrasonography showed a marked reduction in mass size with no detectable flow within the lesion.

CONCLUSION: Penetrating buttock trauma may cause a gluteal pseudoaneurysm with an associated AVF supplied by more than one internal iliac artery branch. Contrast-enhanced CT and selective angiography are important for recognizing the vascular lesion and delineating all feeding arteries. In this patient, embolization of both the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal arterial feeders achieved complete angiographic occlusion and a favorable clinical outcome, with a markedly smaller mass and no detectable intralesional flow on color Doppler ultrasonography at three months.

item.title: Reductions in PTSD symptom clusters among perinatal and postnatal survivors of intimate partner violence participating in the Heartbeats program.
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [weak match]
Aboutanos M, Wishnoff M, Namoos A et al.

BACKGROUND: Intimate partner violence (IPV) remains a leading cause of injury among women, especially during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Experiencing IPV increases the risk of mental health disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD during the perinatal period is associated with poorer maternal mental health and adverse early child outcomes. Heartbeats (HB) is a hospital-based, community-linked violence intervention program designed to reduce morbidity and mortality among perinatal and postnatal survivors of IPV. HB provides crisis intervention, intensive case management, and counseling to pregnant patients up to 2 years postpartum who have experienced IPV. Given the high burden of mental health concerns in this population, a primary goal of HB is to reduce PTSD symptoms.

METHODS: This study was conducted at a Level 1 trauma center. Participants were identified through IPV-related injury presentations, routine hospital screening, or referrals. Seventy-four participants completed the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) at intake (baseline) and 4 months postbaseline (follow-up). Total PTSD and subscale scores were calculated for intrusion (re-experiencing), avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and alterations in arousal and reactivity (hyperarousal). Paired-samples t tests assessed changes from baseline to follow-up.

RESULTS: Significant reductions were observed in total PTSD symptoms (M=9.16, SD=23.64, p =0.003) and across all subscales: intrusion (re-experiencing; M=2.76, SD=6.19, p <0.001), avoidance (M=1.18, SD=2.90, p <0.001), negative alterations in cognition and mood (M=3.82, SD=8.83, p <0.001), and alterations in arousal and reactivity (hyperarousal; M=2.33, SD=7.25, p =0.008).

CONCLUSIONS: HB program participation was associated with significant reductions in overall PTSD severity and each DSM-5 symptom cluster. These findings support the potential of integrated hospital-based, community-linked programs to improve trauma recovery outcomes among perinatal survivors of IPV.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/Epidemiological; Level III.

item.title: Clinical validation of the DRoPH score: a preoperative tool for estimating reduction difficulty in proximal humerus fractures.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [weak match]
Barthel C, Rudolph F, Pape HC et al.

BACKGROUND: Proximal humerus fractures are common injuries that are frequently associated with considerable technical challenges during surgical reduction and fixation. Although anatomical reduction is crucial for fracture healing and functional recovery, the anticipated difficulty of achieving satisfactory reduction is difficult to estimate preoperatively. The Difficulty of Reduction of Proximal Humerus Fractures (DRoPH) score was recently developed through a structured expert consensus process to estimate anticipated reduction difficulty based on predefined fracture- and patient-related characteristics. The aim of this study was to perform an initial clinical validation of the score.

METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed patients who underwent plate fixation of proximal humerus fractures at a tertiary trauma center between January 2014 and December 2024. DRoPH scores (0-10 points) were stratified into low (0-3), moderate (4-6), and high (7-10) difficulty categories. Validation was based on operative duration, postoperative reduction quality according to the criteria described by Schnetzke et al., and postoperative complications. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to assess the independent association of the DRoPH score with the primary outcomes after adjustment for age, sex, and surgical approach. Inter- and intra-rater reliability were assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC).

RESULTS: Of 1,012 patients treated for proximal humerus fractures, 392 met the inclusion criteria and had complete datasets available for analysis. Of these, 151 (38.5%) were classified as low, 186 (47.4%) as moderate, and 55 (14.0%) as high difficulty according to the DRoPH score. Operative duration increased significantly with increasing DRoPH scores, with an adjusted increase of 7.3 min per score point (95% CI 5.7-9.0; p < 0.001). Reduction quality deteriorated across difficulty categories, and higher DRoPH scores were independently associated with malreduction (OR 1.30 per point, 95% CI 1.12-1.50; p = 0.001). Overall complication rates increased from 15.2% in low-difficulty fractures to 34.5% in high-difficulty fractures, and the DRoPH score remained independently associated with complications in multivariable analysis (OR 1.15 per point, 95% CI 1.03-1.28; p = 0.012). Inter- and intra-rater reliability of the overall DRoPH score were excellent (ICC 0.96 and 0.95, respectively).

CONCLUSION: This study provides initial clinical validation of the DRoPH score as a reliable and clinically applicable tool for estimating reduction difficulty in proximal humerus fracture fixation. Higher DRoPH scores are independently associated with longer operative duration, increased risk of malreduction, and higher complication rates. The score may therefore serve as a useful adjunct for preoperative planning and risk stratification in surgically treated proximal humerus fractures. Further multicenter validation studies are warranted.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

item.title: Designing a hybrid surgical ICU to avoid intrahospital transport in selected critically Ill patients: the CUHK-SZ institutional concept.
item.description:
World J Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma] [weak match]
Tsui BC, Chan HH, Peng M et al.

BACKGROUND: Intrahospital transport for surgery exposes critically ill patients to equipment failure, displacement of tubes and lines, interrupted monitoring, and physiologic instability. Although transport protocols can reduce these hazards, they do not address the underlying physical decoupling of surgical infrastructure from the critical care environment.

OBJECTIVE: This institutional perspective describes the rationale and design of a hybrid surgical ICU planned for the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-SZ) Medical Center: a dedicated clinical space designed to function as both a critical care unit and a procedural suite, bringing surgery to the patient rather than transporting the patient to the operating room (OR). The model is presented as an illustrative, hypothesis-generating concept rather than a validated clinical pathway.

DESIGN CONCEPT: The design concept, which is a patient-centered approach, should guide healthcare delivery in modern medicine by placing the patient at the forefront of all decisions and mobilizing all available resources to serve them. This approach addresses all three domains: personnel, environment, and equipment. Overlapping anesthesiology and critical care competencies support integrated staffing. Connectable ICU rooms, adequate space and electrical capacity, anterooms, and switchable HEPA-filtered positive-pressure ventilation meet environmental requirements. Total intravenous anesthesia, portable surgical platforms, and minimally invasive or robotic techniques reduce dependence on fixed OR infrastructure. At CUHK-SZ, the concept is planned as a prototype in the trauma building using two adjacent ICU rooms with an openable partition and switchable ventilation. Candidate patient groups, procedural levels, and implementation requirements are presented as provisional, expert-derived proposals, and engineering testing and simulated drills are planned before any clinical use.

CONCLUSIONS: The hybrid surgical ICU is a technically plausible option for carefully selected patients at high risk from transport, but its clinical effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness remain unproven. The CUHK-SZ concept is intended to generate hypotheses for prospective evaluation, and its transferability to existing hospitals is likely to depend on incremental adaptation rather than direct replication.

item.title: Comparison of suicidal and accidental fall injury patterns: A 10-year retrospective study in Hong Kong.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI, TBI] [weak match]
Hui LH, Hau ESS, Leung LY et al.

BACKGROUND: Falls from a height are a common cause of major trauma in urban areas. This study aims to investigate the differences in patient characteristics and injury patterns between suicidal and accidental falls from a height in Hong Kong.

METHOD: From 2015-2024, patients aged ≥ 18 years recorded under the 'fall from height ≥ 2 m' category of the trauma registry in a tertiary hospital in Hong Kong were retrospectively reviewed. Patient characteristics and the nature of the falls were noted. Abbreviated injury scale (AIS) was the primary outcome. Injury severity score (ISS), skeletal fractures, clinical parameters and clinical outcomes were secondary outcomes.

RESULTS: Of 268 patients included, 50 were in the suicide group and 218 in the accident group. Patients in the suicide group had significantly higher ISS (median 29, IQR 20-45) and fall heights (median 9.0 m, IQR 6.0-10.0 m) than those in the accident group (ISS median 17, IQR 9-26; median fall height 3.0 m, IQR 2.5-5.0 m; both p < 0.001). Within major trauma patients (defined as ISS>15, n = 157), the suicide group had more serious injuries (defined as AIS ≥3) in the abdomen (41% vs 19%, p = 0.008) and extremities (83% vs 28%, p < 0.001), and less serious injuries in the head and neck (39% vs 62%, p = 0.018). Among the major trauma patients, those in the suicide group had more fractures of the ribs, lumbar spine, pelvis, hips and feet, while those in the accident group sustained more skull fractures. In particular, all deaths in the accident group had AIS head and neck ≥ 5. Subgroup analysis according to fall height in the major trauma cases found the differences in pelvic fractures between the two groups remained significant in falls < 10 m.

CONCLUSION: Falls from heights due to accidents more often result in serious head injuries, while those due to suicide more often have serious injuries in the lower part of the body. Serious head injury is a major cause of death in accidental falls.

item.title: Injury patterns in a war zone: A comparative analysis of civilians and military personnel.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [weak match]
Sasson I, Chaushu H, Ungar OJ

BACKGROUND: Modern armed conflicts increasingly affect both civilians and defense forces, resulting in heterogeneous injury patterns driven by diverse mechanisms. Direct comparative data between these populations treated within the same healthcare system remain limited.

OBJECTIVE: To compare injury mechanisms, anatomical injury patterns, injury severity, and early clinical outcomes between civilians and defense forces casualties treated at a single tertiary trauma center during an active conflict.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted of all consecutive war-related trauma admissions between October 7, 2023, and January 7, 2024. Demographic data, injury mechanisms, anatomical sites, Injury Severity Score (ISS), emergency interventions, and early outcomes were collected. Percentage-based comparative plots were used to visualize injury mechanism and anatomical site distributions.

RESULTS: The cohort included 192 patients (128 defense forces, 64 civilians). Civilians were older and included more females. Overall injury severity and rates of airway management, ventilatory support, and ICU admission were comparable between groups. Defense forces more frequently required direct transfer from the emergency department to the operating room (28% vs. 14%, p = 0.047). Shrapnel-related injuries were significantly more common among defense forces, whereas acoustic trauma was observed exclusively among civilians (36%, p < 0.001). Injury-mechanism profiles differed between groups, whereas no statistically significant differences were observed in the proportions of patients injured at the individual anatomical site.

CONCLUSIONS: Despite similar overall injury severity, civilians and defense forces exhibit distinct injury profiles. Civilians are disproportionately affected by acoustic trauma, highlighting population-specific vulnerabilities with implications for triage, diagnostic evaluation, and trauma system preparedness, especially during mass casualty incidents, when rapid recognition of group-specific injury patterns is essential for appropriate resource prioritization and allocation.

item.title: Early post-ROSC laboratory phenotypes and clinical outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a 10-year national cohort study.
item.description:
Resuscitation | Tier 2 Filtered [Prehospital] [weak match]
Liu X, Chong KW, Lau YH et al.

BACKGROUND: Prior phenotyping in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) relied predominantly on prehospital indicators, which neither describe nor grade the underlying ischemia-reperfusion injury. We aimed to derive laboratory-based phenotypes and describe their clinical characteristics and outcome associations.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult resuscitated OHCA patients of presumed cardiac etiology between 01/02/2011 and 01/01/2022, linking Singapore's national OHCA and cardiovascular databases. Unsupervised latent class analysis (LCA) was applied to 14 laboratory variables within six hours post-return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Stability was confirmed through split-sample validation. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for age, sex and initial cardiac rhythm, assessed poor neurological recovery at hospital discharge, 30-day and 3-year mortality.

RESULTS: Among 1514 eligible patients (median age 65.0 years, 73.6% males), LCA identified three distinct phenotypes: multi-organ dysfunction (MOD, N = 286), homeostatic (HOM, N = 967), and immune-dysregulated (IMD, N = 261), independently reproduced in derivation (entropy = 0.817) and replication (entropy = 0.892) subsamples. The most discriminative variables were creatinine, eosinophil and lymphocyte. Compared to MOD, both HOM (aOR: 0.50, 95% CI 0.30-0.78, p = 0.004) and IMD (aOR: 0.46, 95% CI 0.26-0.78, p = 0.005) phenotypes had significantly lower odds of poor neurological recovery. This pattern was consistent for 30-day mortality (HOM aHR: 0.71, 95% CI 0.61-0.83; IMD aHR: 0.78, 95% CI 0.64-0.94) and 3-year mortality (HOM aHR: 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.82; IMD aHR: 0.74, 95% CI 0.62-0.90), all p ≤ 0.01.

CONCLUSION: Early post-ROSC laboratory data identified three prognostically distinct phenotypes among resuscitated OHCA patients. These exploratory findings support external validation and investigation of phenotype-guided therapies.

item.title: Force measurement in circular external fixation frames reflects construct stability: A laboratory proof-of-concept study.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Naeem H, Maroy R, Stewart T et al.

BACKGROUND: Circular external fixation frames are widely used in limb reconstruction, however determining the optimal time for frame removal remains challenging. Current approaches rely on clinical and radiological assessment, both of which have recognised limitations. Mechanical assessment of construct stability offers a potential alternative, but existing approaches have not translated widely into clinical practice, in part due to reliance on absolute measurement thresholds.

OBJECTIVE: To determine whether force measurement within a circular external fixation frame varies systematically with fracture site stability, and to assess whether this measurement may support monitoring of healing progression.

METHODS: Three similar four-ring Ilizarov frame constructs were assembled using a Perspex bone analogue. A load cell was integrated into the frame and used to measure force during axial loading to 700 N. Models representing different stages of fracture healing were simulated using varying fracture gaps and materials of differing stiffness. Measurements were obtained across multiple sensor positions and configurations. Force measurements were compared between models using non-parametric statistical methods. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to assess separation between conditions.

RESULTS: Force measured within the frame decreased progressively with increasing construct stiffness. A significant relationship between model stability and measured force was observed (Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.0001). Clear separation was demonstrated between grossly unstable and intact constructs; however, overlap between higher stability models and intact bone was evident. ROC analysis showed strong discrimination when considering all unstable conditions (AUC ≥ 0.91), but performance was reduced when restricted to higher stability models (AUC 0.699-0.838). Absolute force measurements varied with sensor configuration, although the rank order of conditions was preserved.

CONCLUSION: Force measurement within a circular external fixation frame reflects construct stability in an in vitro model. Whilst absolute values are dependent on construct configuration and show reduced discrimination near union, consistent directional changes suggest that serial within-subject measurement may provide a useful approach to monitoring healing progression. These findings support further evaluation of longitudinal measurement strategies in clinical studies.

item.title: Screening for posttraumatic stress symptoms after accidental injury: Implementation of the young child PTSD screen in the acute trauma setting.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Paediatric, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Ray M, Bailey A, Lendrum E et al.

BACKGROUND: Post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) in young children are underrecognized following unintentional injury, and validated screening tools for early childhood are rarely implemented in acute trauma settings. We evaluated the Young Child PTSD Screen (YCPS) administered at hospital discharge to determine screening positivity, associated clinical factors, and persistence of symptoms at one month.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of children aged 2-6 years admitted to a Level I pediatric trauma center following unintentional injury (November 2020-November 2024). Caregivers completed the 6-item YCPS at discharge. Children with ≥ 1 endorsed symptom were contacted one month later for repeat assessment. Demographic, injury, and hospitalization data were abstracted from the trauma registry and electronic health record. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated predictors of positive screening at discharge, and follow-up analyses assessed persistence of symptoms.

RESULTS: Of 193 screened patients, 186 met inclusion criteria. Over half (55.9%, n = 104) screened symptomatic or positive at discharge. On univariate analysis, greater injury severity score and longer length of stay were associated with symptomatic/positive screening. In multivariable analysis, injury severity remained the only significant predictor (aOR 1.07 per point increase in injury severity score, 95% CI 1.02-1.13, p = 0.004). Of eligible children, 32.6% (n = 34) completed one-month follow-up and 41.1% (n = 14) screened positive. Higher discharge YCPS scores were associated with positive follow-up (median 3 vs 2; p = 0.046) and were positively correlated with one-month scores (r²=0.21, p = 0.005). No demographic variables (age, sex, race) predicted persistence of symptoms.

CONCLUSIONS: Over one-third of traumatically injured young children screened positive for PTSS at discharge, and a substantial proportion had persistent symptoms at one month. Injury severity was associated with positive screens at discharge, while early symptom burden predicted persistence. These findings support the feasibility and clinical value of implementing developmentally sensitive screening for very young children in the inpatient trauma setting.

item.title: Clinical equipoise as inclusion criterion to control for confounding in observational studies.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]
van der Hoeven NM, Peuker F, Michelitsch C et al.

PURPOSE: This study investigates whether higher levels of expert disagreement, as a proxy for clinical equipoise, are associated with improved baseline comparability between treatment groups in patients with proximal humerus fractures. Additionally, it aimed to assess how progressively stricter inclusion criteria-based on this disagreement-affect the distribution of baseline characteristics between the treatment groups.

METHODS: We used data from the LADON Humerus study, a multicentre, prospective cohort including patients treated operatively or non-operatively in five hospitals in the Netherlands and Switzerland. An international expert panel of trauma surgeons assessed anonymized cases, blinded to the actual treatment, and each expert gave a treatment recommendation. Disagreement between the treatment given and the expert recommendations was categorized into four levels (A: complete disagreement, B: partial disagreement, C: partial agreement, D: complete agreement). Standardized differences (StDiff) for age, sex, ASA score, and AO classification were used to assess comparability between treatment groups across disagreement levels.

RESULTS: A total of 351 patients were included in the analysis. Comparability between treatment groups improved as the level of disagreement increased. At complete disagreement (Level A), the groups were well balanced with respect to age, sex, and ASA score (StDiff ≤ 0.1). For AO classification, group comparability improved but remained insufficiently balanced at the highest level of disagreement. Stricter inclusion criteria resulted in improved balance at the cost of reduced sample size.

CONCLUSION: Using expert panel disagreement as inclusion criterion can enhance group comparability in observational research. This approach may reduce the potential for confounding when RCTs are not possible.

item.title: Diagnostic accuracy of shock index, revised trauma score, and injury severity score for mortality prediction in trauma: A hierarchical meta-analysis.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Raza AA, Ahmad M, Choudhary N et al.

BACKGROUND: Shock Index (SI) and Revised Trauma Score (RTS) are physiological tools available at the point of trauma triage. Injury Severity Score (ISS) is an anatomical score that requires completed injury characterization and is typically available only after initial resuscitation. Their comparative value for predicting mortality and whether ISS meaningfully adds to the acute tools remains unclear.

AIMS: The aim of this systematic review and hierarchical meta-analysis is to pool the diagnostic accuracy of SI and RTS as acute mortality-prediction tools in adult trauma patients; to benchmark these against ISS; and to formally test, in studies reporting both, whether RTS and ISS differ in diagnostic accuracy.

METHODS: Electronic databases were searched from inception to May 2026. In-hospital mortality was prespecified as the primary endpoint. Pooled sensitivity, specificity and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) analyses were performed with a bivariate random-effects model for each tool separately. For studies reporting both RTS and ISS in the same cohort, a paired comparison was performed using a bivariate model with test type as a covariate and a pooled within-study difference analysis.

RESULTS: Twelve studies (234,129 patients) were included. Pooled sensitivity/specificity were 0.679/0.763 for SI (5 studies, AUC 0.747), 0.788/0.801 for RTS (6 studies, AUC 0.852), and 0.788/0.796 for ISS (9 studies, AUC 0.855). In the six studies reporting both RTS and ISS, a paired bivariate comparison found no significant difference in diagnostic accuracy (likelihood-ratio test, p = 0.91; within-study sensitivity OR 1.59, 95% CI 0.82-3.07; specificity OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.55-1.45).

CONCLUSION: RTS and ISS did not differ significantly in a formal paired comparison, and neither tool, alone, reliably rules in or out death at realistic trauma prevalence. SI, RTS and ISS should be understood as serving different, complementary roles across the trauma timeline - SI and RTS at the point of acute triage, ISS as a later anatomical benchmark - rather than as competing predictors to be ranked against one another.

item.title: Epidemiological patterns and surgical outcomes of pediatric supracondylar humerus fractures: a focus on domestic safety and seasonal variations.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Altin R, Cakirturk S, Erten RA et al.

INTRODUCTION: Supracondylar humerus fractures (SHFs) are prevalent pediatric elbow injuries. This study investigates the epidemiology, clinical characteristics, and treatment outcomes of pediatric SHFs to identify preventive strategies.

METHODS: This retrospective study included 298 pediatric patients (aged ≤14 years) treated for SHFs between December 2018 and June 2024. Demographic data, injury mechanisms, seasonal variations, and surgical details were analyzed. Radiological reduction was assessed via the Baumann angle and anterior humeral line. Functional outcomes were evaluated using Flynn's criteria.

RESULTS: The study cohort (mean age 6.1 years; 58.7% male) predominantly sustained extension-type fractures (96.3%), with the severely displaced Gartland Type III being the most frequent (49.3%). The incidence of injuries peaked during the summer months and school holidays, with the majority occurring at home (64.1%) due to simple falls (93%). Surgical intervention, consisting of closed reduction and percutaneous pinning, was necessitated in 75.8% of cases, with a mean time-to-surgery of 4.6 h. Satisfactory (excellent and good) functional outcomes were achieved in 97.9% of the patients. Overall complication rates were minimal, and transient nerve injuries (2%) fully resolved spontaneously during follow-up.

CONCLUSION: Pediatric SHFs frequently occur in domestic settings during the summer months, strongly highlighting the need for "safe home" modifications and parental education. Despite a high prevalence of severely displaced fractures, prompt surgical intervention and meticulous anatomical reduction yield excellent long-term functional outcomes and minimize complications.

item.title: Renal trauma in a pediatric Level 1 trauma center: morbidity, mortality, and the role of renal scintigraphy.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Paediatric, Systems/QI, TBI] [strong match]
Jansen SAM, Haouli B, Backes M et al.

PURPOSE: Pediatric renal trauma is uncommon but potentially serious, and is often managed conservatively. Complications may occur, and the clinical value of renal scintigraphy during follow-up remains unclear. This study aimed to assess morbidity and mortality after pediatric renal trauma and to assess the clinical value of renal scintigraphy during follow-up.

METHODS: This retrospective single-center cohort study included pediatric trauma patients (< 18 years) with renal injuries admitted to a Level 1 trauma center in the Netherlands between January 1, 2001, and December 31, 2024. Mortality and in-hospital complications were assessed, and associations between renal scintigraphy abnormalities and complications during follow-up were evaluated.

RESULTS: A total of 72 patients were included, of whom all injuries resulted from blunt trauma. Conservative management was applied in 88% of cases; embolization and nephrectomy were performed in 8% and 3% of patients, respectively. In-hospital mortality was 11% and was attributed exclusively to concomitant traumatic brain injury. Complications occurred in 25% of patients, primarily infections (19%), followed by hypertension during follow up (4%). Renal scintigraphy was performed in 53% of patients, predominantly in those with high-grade injuries; abnormalities were frequently observed (77%) but did not correlate with the occurrence of hypertension, proteinuria, or renal insufficiency during follow-up.

CONCLUSION: Pediatric renal trauma, including high-grade injuries, can often be managed conservatively, and most complications can be treated using medical therapy or minimally invasive interventions. Renal scintigraphy showed no clear association with long-term morbidity and had limited additional value in routine follow-up. Given the potential for late-onset hypertension, structured long-term clinical surveillance with periodic monitoring of blood pressure, proteinuria, and renal function is warranted, particularly after high-grade injuries.

item.title: Measurement properties of pulmonary function measurement and patient-reported outcome measures in patients with multiple rib fracture without flail segment; validation study alongside the multicenter FixCon trial.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Thoracic] [strong match]
Luttjeboer ML, Van Diepen MR, Prins JTH et al.

BACKGROUND: The reliability and validity of pulmonary function, pain and health related quality of life (HR-QoL) as outcome measures for patients with rib fractures, remain uncertain. Our objective was to evaluate measurement properties in patients with multiple rib fractures by comparing them with generic HR-QoL instruments (EuroQoL-5D-5L [EQ-5D-5L], Short Form-12 [SF-12]).

METHODS: A multicenter RCT in adults (n = 180) was performed. Spirometry was performed at 30 days, 3, 6, and 12 months after trauma. Patients completed five questions on pain, EQ-5D-5L, SF-12, and two anchor questions on improvement in pulmonary function and thoracic complaints since previous measurement. Reliability, construct validity, responsiveness and floor and ceiling effects were evaluated for all follow-up time-points.

RESULTS: EQ-5D and SF-12 (sub)scales showed adequate internal consistency. Construct and longitudinal validity were adequate for all (sub)scales, except for construct validity of the SF-12 Physical Component Summary. Ceiling effects were present for all pain questions from 30 days onwards, for EQ-5D-5L utility score (US) from 3 months onwards. Responsiveness analysis indicated that spirometry values showed trivial (tidal volume), small (inspiratory capacity, FEV1), or moderate (FVC) degree of change from 30 days to 12 months. All five pain levels, EQ-5D-5L and SF-12 (sub)scales showed moderate to large degree of change form 30 days to 12 months.

CONCLUSIONS: Spirometry and pain are valid instruments for monitoring functional recovery in patients after sustaining multiple rib fractures. Responsiveness was confirmed for pain and spirometry (FVC). EQ-5D-5L and SF-12 are valid, reliable, and responsive. Pain and HRQoL are therefore suitable instruments for measuring treatment effects over time.

item.title: Prehospital severity and in-hospital mortality in trauma patients managed by the Friuli-Venezia Giulia helicopter emergency medical service: a 6-year retrospective cohort study.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Prehospital, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Tomasino S, Pegani C, Orso D et al.

BACKGROUND: Data on in-hospital mortality among trauma patients managed by Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) in Italy remain limited. We aimed to describe the epidemiology and in-hospital mortality of trauma patients transported after management by the Friuli-Venezia Giulia HEMS and to assess prehospital factors associated with death.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study including trauma patients managed by HEMS FVG and transported to hospital, either directly by HEMS or after continuation of transport by ground emergency medical services, between 2018 and 2023. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Jeffreys-prior penalized logistic regression was used to reduce sparse-data bias and instability from separation. The RTS-based model was designated as the primary model and the NACA-based model as a secondary sensitivity analysis. Model performance was assessed internally, and the functional forms of both age and RTS were examined using restricted cubic splines.

RESULTS: Of 3,357 trauma records in the source cohort, 205 prehospital deaths were excluded from the in-hospital mortality analysis, leaving 3,152 transported patients. Outcome data were available for 3,143 patients, of whom 107 died in hospital (3.4%). In the primary RTS-based model, older age, lower RTS, tracheal intubation, and prehospital CPR were associated with mortality. Compared with RTS ≥ 7, adjusted ORs were 2.36 (95% CI 1.11-5.50) for RTS 4-<7 and 5.19 (95% CI 1.64-17.04) for RTS < 4. Age was associated with mortality (OR 1.03 per year, 95% CI 1.01-1.04). Continuous RTS analysis was concordant (OR 0.68 per one-point increase, 95% CI 0.54-0.86; p = 0.0013).

CONCLUSIONS: Among trauma patients transported to hospital after HEMS management, older age, higher prehospital injury severity, tracheal intubation, and prehospital CPR were associated with in-hospital mortality. Intubation and CPR should be interpreted primarily as markers of severe physiological compromise rather than causal determinants of death.

item.title: Survival benefit of prehospital TXA in fibrinolytic shutdown: Insights from two prospective trauma trials.
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Haemorrhage, Prehospital, Systems/QI, TBI] [strong match]
Kenny JE, Brito AM, Benchiba-Charron M et al.

BACKGROUND: Fibrinolytic phenotypes have been implicated in postinjury pathophysiology and outcomes. While prehospital tranexamic acid (TXA) administration has demonstrated survival benefits, the interaction between TXA administration and distinct fibrinolytic profiles remains poorly defined.

METHODS: We analyzed data from a harmonized dataset combining 2 prospective trials evaluating prehospital TXA use in trauma (Prehospital Tranexamic Acid Use for Traumatic Brain Injury and the Study of Tranexamic Acid During Air and Ground Medical Prehospital Transport Trial). Patients were stratified by initial thromboelastographic (TEG) LY30 into fibrinolytic shutdown (<0.9%), hyperfibrinolysis (>3%), and physiological fibrinolysis (0.9-3%). The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included 24-hour mortality and adverse events. Multivariable regression adjusted for TXA administration, fibrinolysis phenotypes, age, mechanism of injury, injury severity score, and shock index on presentation to the hospital.

RESULTS: Among 1,249 patients, 30-day mortality was 14.5% in the fibrinolytic shutdown group, 6.7% in the hyperfibrinolysis group, and 6.5% in the physiological fibrinolysis group. After multivariable regression, hyperfibrinolysis was associated with increased risk of death (HR 2.87; 95% CI: 1.10-7.53; p 0.03). Patients with fibrinolytic shutdown who were randomized to TXA had decreased risk of death (HR 0.32; 95% CI: 0.11-0.91; p=0.03).

CONCLUSIONS: This multitrial analysis revealed greater statistically significant differences between fibrinolytic phenotypes than analysis of each trial alone. Fibrinolytic phenotypes were independently associated with mortality. Fibrinolytic shutdown in patients randomized to receive TXA was associated with lower risk of death. These findings support the relevance of fibrinolysis profiling during early trauma care and underscore the need for larger studies to further elucidate the prognostic and therapeutic implications in trauma.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II (Subanalysis of Randomized Controlled Trials).

item.title: Decompressive craniectomy: The potential association with long-term functional outcomes in children with traumatic brain injury.
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, TBI] [strong match]
Wong AM, Braschi CD, Matsushima K

BACKGROUND: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in pediatric patients. However, TBI management widely varies due to a lack of high-quality evidence in pediatric population. We aimed to determine the association of decompressive craniectomy (DC) on long-term functional independence in pediatric TBI. We hypothesize that the use of DC would not be associated with improved functional independence after discharge.

METHODS: This is a retrospective cohort study using the Federal Interagency Traumatic Brain Injury Research (FITBIR) Informatics System, a national database of TBI studies. The Approaches and Decisions in Acute Pediatric TBI (ADAPT) Trial was selected for its international patient population from 2014 to 2017. Patients (age ≤18 y) with TBI, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ≤8, and insertion of an intracranial pressure monitor were categorized into the DC and no-DC groups. The primary outcome was Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended Pediatric Version (GOS-E Peds) at a follow-up visit ≥6 months postdischarge. A secondary analysis included all patients admitted for the management of TBI to examine the association between DC and in-hospital mortality.

RESULTS: We included 686 TBI patients followed up ≥6 months postdischarge or recorded mortality. Of those, 213 (31.0%) patients received DC. The median GCS on presentation was 5. The median GOS-E at follow-up was 5. In a multivariate regression model, the use of DC was not associated with good functional recovery defined as GOS-E Peds <5 (odds ratio [OR]: 0.64, 95% CI: 0.39-1.05, p=0.077). In a secondary analysis, DC was not associated with in-hospital mortality (OR: 1.02, 95% CI: 0.60-1.74, p=0.95).

CONCLUSION: The results of this study suggest that DC is not significantly associated with favorable functional outcomes >6 months postdischarge or decreased in-hospital mortality. Future research is warranted to further delineate the indication for DC in the pediatric TBI population.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/epidemiological study; Level IV.

item.title: Does Surgeon Experience Affect Outcomes in Robotic Cholecystectomy for Emergency Biliary Disease? A Statewide Analysis.
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [weak match]
Levy SC, Johnson PL, Zambito M et al.

BACKGROUND: The use of robotic surgery (RS) as an operative technique in emergency general surgery (EGS) is rapidly growing, with a >3-fold increase in RS-EGS operations since 2011. Prior work has utilized payer claims to evaluate outcomes of RS-cholecystectomy in the EGS setting. However, these studies fail to evaluate how outcomes are affected by surgeon experience or whether there is a learning curve for RS in the EGS setting. We hypothesized that surgeons on the learning curve may have higher rates of complications.

METHODS: EGS collaborative data from 12 hospitals were used to compare the postoperative outcomes of patients undergoing RS-cholecystectomy to those undergoing laparoscopic (LS) cholecystectomy. Unadjusted and adjusted outcomes were compared between the control (LS) and the exposure (RS) groups, using entropy balancing and multivariable analysis. Learning curves were plotted for postoperative outcomes, operative time, and hospital length of stay, using linear spline curve modeling (single knot at case 70) to represent how outcomes change with increasing surgeon experience.

RESULTS: We evaluated 8,221 minimally invasive total cholecystectomy cases, of which 2,141 were performed with RS. RS-cholecystectomy was associated with a lower rate of technical complications, independent of surgeon experience (adjusted odds ratio: 0.38, 95% CI: 0.21-0.69, p=0.002). Operative time was longer, and nontechnical complications were higher for RS-cholecystectomy (+13.1min, 95% CI: 7.3-18.8, p<0.001 and adjusted odds ratio: 1.18, 95% CI: 1.01-1.39, P=0.043, respectively). Adjusted operative time decreased by 14.1 minutes over the first 70 cases (95% CI: -21.8 to -6.4, p<0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: RS-cholecystectomy is not associated with more technical complications, and surgeons with less RS experience did not have a higher likelihood of technical complications for cholecystectomy when compared with LS in an EGS setting. Operative times for RS-cholecystectomy are longer than LS and significantly decrease with increasing surgeon experience.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic/Care Management; Level III.

STUDY TYPE: Prognostic/epidemiological.

item.title: Prehospital transport prioritization and time-varying selection bias in traffic-related multi-patient incidents: a nationwide retrospective cohort study.
item.description:
Crit Care | Tier 2 Filtered [Prehospital, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Kubo A, Tamura S, Hiraide A et al.

BACKGROUND: In prehospital multi-patient traffic incidents, the first ambulance to depart -priority transport - may reflect underlying injury severity rather than a treatment effect, as more severely injured patients are systematically prioritized. Conventional statistical methods often fail to separate this severity-dependent selection from actual outcomes. We applied a "doubly robust" statistical framework (augmented inverse probability weighting, AIPW), which combines a treatment model and an outcome model, to better account for measured differences, reduce selection bias, and examine whether on-scene time modifies this association.

METHODS: We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using emergency medical service transport records from the Fire and Disaster Management Agency of Japan (January 2021-December 2023). Of 13,821,224 records, 143,130 patients from traffic-related multi-patient incidents (TMIs; ≥2 patients per incident) with complete data were included. The exposure was priority transport. The primary outcome was physician-assessed death or critical/severe injury at hospital arrival. Marginal adjusted risk differences (RDs) were estimated using AIPW. Effect modification by on-scene time (5-60 min) was assessed by marginal standardization with cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. Sensitivity analyses included overlap restriction and E-value quantification of unmeasured confounding.

RESULTS: Among 143,130 patients (median age 41 years; female, 50.57%), 62,769 (43.85%) underwent priority transport. Severe outcomes occurred in 4.35% of priority and 1.87% of non-priority patients. The overall RDs was 2.2% points (95% CI, 2.01-2.36). A significant interaction with on-scene time was observed (p < .001): the marginal RD was peaked at 5 min (6.4% points; 95% CI, 5.6-7.2), declined to a minimum of 1.4% points (95% CI, 1.3-1.6) at approximately 32 min, and increased modestly to 2.4% points (95% CI, 2.0-2.8) at 60 min. Sensitivity analyses confirmed result robustness, yielding an E-value of 3.76 (lower bound, 3.57).

CONCLUSIONS: The association between priority transport and severe outcome was modified by on-scene time, with the largest risk difference at the shortest on-scene times. This U-shaped pattern is consistent with preferential selection of more severely injured patients for rapid transport, rather than a direct effect of transport order. Accounting for prehospital triage selection when interpreting transport-outcome associations in critical care research.
